THIRTY YEARS OF 2D MIT

Sergey V. Kravchenkoa, Vladimir M. Pudalovb, and Alexander A. Shashkinc ††thanks: CONTACT S.˜V. Kravchenko. Email: s.kravchenko@northeastern.edu
Abstract

The zero-magnetic-field metal-insulator transition in strongly correlated two-dimensional electron systems was experimentally discovered three decades ago, thereby triggering extensive experimental and theoretical investigations. Prior to this discovery, the occurrence of such a transition — as well as the very existence of a metallic phase in two dimensions — was regarded as forbidden within the framework of the one-parameter scaling theory of localization. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of the transport and thermodynamic properties of two-dimensional electron and hole systems in which carrier-carrier interactions constitute the dominant energy scale. We present and critically analyze both experimental observations and theoretical developments accumulated over the past thirty years.

keywords
Metal-insulator transition, two-dimensional electron systems, strong correlations, Wigner crystal

1 Introduction

The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in three-dimensional bulk materials was pioneered by Sir Nevill Mott, who established the foundations of our understanding of this phenomenon. It remains one of the most challenging problems in condensed matter physics, especially in lower dimensional systems that have become accessible by advances in technology since Mott’s time.

The discovery in the mid-1990s of the metallic-like transport in two-dimensional (2D) strongly interacting electron systems and of its critical behavior at the verge of the transition to the hopping-type transport sparked an explosion of interest among theorists and experimentalists. Furthermore, it revealed a critical deficiency in the existing harmonious structure of knowledge developed primarily by Mott [1], Anderson [2], and Abrahams et al. [3], as well as in the concepts of quantum transport in strongly correlated systems. Understanding the mechanisms of metal-like transport, the nature of the ground state, and the properties of strongly interacting electron systems is essential for modeling the observed phenomena. The identified knowledge gap prompted a marked increase in both theoretical and experimental research, leading to a comprehensive revision of existing concepts in this field. This has led to a new understanding of the quantum physics of strongly interacting 2D electron systems. As a consequence of this influx of research, new theoretical ideas and experimental methods have been developed, revealing several unique features in the thermodynamics and kinetics of low-dimensional systems comprising charged fermions.

The purpose of this review is to introduce the reader to the world of vivid, exciting, and sometimes unforeseen effects that manifest themselves in strongly interacting systems, as well as to the foundations of the theoretical description of their properties. Indeed, this discovery for 2D systems forced us to re-examine the properties not only of transport but, more generally, of quantum kinetics and thermodynamics in strongly correlated electron systems, far beyond the frameworks of the Fermi liquid model.

We will focus on several interconnected phenomena in strongly correlated 2D electron systems. These include the temperature-dependent metallic conductivity, the transition between metal and insulator, a strong increase in spin susceptibility and effective mass near the transition, and collective transport in the insulating state. We will also review several theoretical approaches proposed to explain the observed phenomena.

The review is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present the main theoretical concepts and experimental results on quantum transport prior to the discovery of the 2D MIT. In Section 3, the major experimental results on metallic transport and the zero-field metal-insulator transition in strongly interacting 2D electron and hole systems are presented. Section 4 is devoted to the suppression of the coherent backscattering on the metallic side near the metal-insulator transition. In Section 5, we show that two independent approaches to determining the critical electron density for the MIT yield the same result. In Sections 6 and 7, the effects of the parallel and perpendicular magnetic fields are considered. In Section 8, we examine the significant increase and potential divergence of both spin susceptibility and effective electron mass, as indicated by transport and thermodynamic measurements. In Section 9, we present the argument that, on the insulating side of the metal-insulator transition, there exists an electron solid that closely resembles a pinned Wigner crystal in many aspects. Finally, Section 10 reviews modern theoretical approaches to the 2D MIT.

2 Weak and strong localization: early theory and experiments

In 2D electron systems, the electrons are confined to move in a plane in the presence of a random potential. The end of the 70s and the beginning of the 80s witnessed a triumph of the one-parameter scaling theory of localization [3, 4, 5] and the theory of electron-electron interactions in disordered conductors [6, 7] (for a review, see Ref. [8]). Charge carriers are always localized in one dimension; electronic states can be either localized or extended in three dimensions, and the absence of extended states is predicted in two-dimensional systems in the limit of zero temperature. In two dimensions, electrons may conduct well at room temperature, but a weak logarithmic increase in resistance is expected as the temperature is reduced in the metallic-conductivity regime at high electron densities. This is because, when scattered by impurities back to their starting point, electron waves interfere constructively with their time-reversed counterparts. Although these effects are negligible at high temperatures due to inelastic scattering, quantum interference becomes significant as the temperature is reduced, leading to the so-called “weak localization”. The terms “weak localization” and “strong localization” are commonly used to denote states that exhibit logarithmic (in the 2D case) and exponential (in any dimension) temperature dependence of resistance.

Furthermore, weak electron-electron interactions introduce a separate set of corrections to conductivity σ\sigma that can either enhance or counteract the effect depending on the value of the interaction constant F0σF_{0}^{\sigma} in the triplet channel, which depends on the interaction strength [7, 9, 10, 11, 8]:

δ​σ=−e22​π2​ℏ​ln⁡(ℏkB​T​τ)​[1+3​(1−ln⁡(1+F0σ)F0σ)],\delta\sigma=-\frac{e^{2}}{2\pi^{2}\hbar}\ln\left(\frac{\hbar}{k_{B}T\tau}\right)\Big[1+3\left(1-\frac{\ln(1+F_{0}^{\sigma})}{F_{0}^{\sigma}}\right)\Big], (1)

where kBk_{B} is the Boltzmann constant, TT is the temperature, and τ\tau is the mean free time. Indeed, thin metallic films and 2D electron systems fabricated on semiconductor interfaces were found to display the predicted logarithmic increase in resistivity with decreasing temperature [12, 13, 14], providing support for the weak localization theory (Figs. 1 and 2).

In 2D electron systems with significant disorder, which inevitably arises at very low electron densities, the localization becomes strong. The resistance displays an activation temperature dependence (see, e.g., Ref. [14] and Fig. 3) that at very low temperatures switches to a R∝exp⁡((T0/T)1/2)R\propto\exp((T_{0}/T)^{1/2}) temperature dependence [15] corresponding to a variable-range hopping regime.

Given the remarkable agreement between theory and experiment, the description of the electronic properties of 2D electron systems seemed well-defined at that time. However, from time to time, indications appeared that the accepted view might not always be correct, as discussed in the next section.

3 Zero-magnetic-field metal-insulator transition in strongly interacting 2D electron systems

3.1 Temperature dependence of the resistivity in Si MOSFETs

Curiously, applying these ideas to the 2D electron liquid in silicon metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) — one of the most ubiquitous 2D systems — remained a challenge. In the early experiments [16] with low-mobility (∼0.1CLOSE(\sim 0.1 m2/Vs) structures in the regime of relatively high electron densities (ns>1012n_{s}>10^{12} cm-2), a decrease of the conductivity with cooling was observed, apparently in qualitative agreement with the ideas of weak localization and electron-electron interactions [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. However, quantitatively describing this behavior was problematic [17]. The disagreement with the theory became qualitative with the advent of moderate-mobility (up to ≈2\approx 2\,m2/Vs) structures: the low-TT conductivity σ\sigma in such Si MOSFETs increased as temperature decreased [18, 19, 20]. This seemingly metallic behavior of the conductivity is especially pronounced at low electron densities ns∼(1−2)×1011n_{s}\sim(1-2)\times 10^{11} cm-2, where a five-fold decrease of ρ\rho with cooling was observed [21].

The strength of the electron-electron interactions is characterized by the ratio between the Coulomb and Fermi energies, which in a single-valley case is equal to

rs=1/(π​ns)1/2​aBr_{s}=1/(\pi n_{s})^{1/2}a_{B} (2)

(here aBa_{B} is the Bohr radius in a semiconductor). In the early experiments [12, 16, 13, 14], the Coulomb interactions are relatively weak. As the electron density decreases, the ratio of Coulomb energy to Fermi energy increases. Consequently, interactions become the primary energy scale in the system. No comprehensive analytical theory existed for the strongly-interacting limit (rs≫1r_{s}\gg 1) at the time when the 2D metal-insulator transition was experimentally observed. To our knowledge, only Finkel’stein [9, 10] and Castellani et al. [11] have proposed that a two-dimensional system with weak disorder and sufficiently strong interactions will be in a conducting state as the temperature decreases.

However, this scaling process increases the effective interaction strength, leading to a divergent spin susceptibility. As a result, the perturbative approach breaks down as the temperature approaches zero. Therefore, the possibility of a stable 2D metallic ground state driven by strong electron-electron interactions was not given serious consideration, particularly because of the lack of experimental confirmation.

Advances in semiconductor technology have enabled the fabrication of high-quality two-dimensional samples with very low disorder, thereby allowing measurements at extremely low carrier densities. As a result, the strongly interacting regime (rs≫1r_{s}\gg 1) became experimentally accessible. The initial report on the substantial metallic temperature dependence of resistance and the two-dimensional metal-insulator transition in nn- and pp-Si MOSFETs (Zavaritskaya and Zavaritskaya [21]) received little attention. However, numerous experimental results from various research groups suggested that a metallic state may be possible in two dimensions. Pudalov et al. [22, 23, 24] and Shashkin et al. [25, 26, 27] studied the phase diagram of the quantum Hall effect (QHE) in low-disordered Si MOSFETs and GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures and have come to the conclusion that a metal-insulator transition exists in clean samples. In a strong magnetic field, each Landau level comprises a set of states with an energy spread due to disorder. The conventional view is that these states are all localized except for those at the center of each Landau level, which are extended. In the limit of a vanishing magnetic field, these extended states are expected to float up indefinitely in energy [28, 29], thus making the 2D system insulating. However, the authors of Refs. [22, 25, 26, 23, 24] have found, contrary to expectations, that the extended states do not float up indefinitely in the limit of zero magnetic field, but coalesce instead at finite energies, thus allowing for a metallic state at B=0B=0.

Later, in 1994-1996, strong metallic temperature dependences with the sevenfold decrease in resistivity at temperatures ≲2.5\lesssim 2.5 K were observed in high-mobility Si MOSFET samples [30, 31], revealing dramatic differences in the behavior of strongly interacting 2D systems with rs>10r_{s}>10 compared to weakly interacting systems. As the electron density increased, the systems transitioned from a regime in which resistance diverged as temperature decreased (indicating insulating behavior) to one in which resistance decreased with decreasing temperature (indicating strongly metallic behavior) (see Fig. 4). The two regimes are separated by the line at a critical electron density, ncn_{c} (dashed red line in Fig. 4), which has a weak temperature dependence and extrapolates to approximately 3​h/e23h/e^{2} as the temperature tends to zero. 11 1 Care should be taken to prevent the electron system from overheating at millikelvin temperatures due to external electromagnetic interference. Common experimental techniques include dedicated grounding, proper shielding and screening of the measurement circuits, filtering out pickup and noise, and using optocouplers and battery-operated preamplifiers.

3.1.1 High- and low-mobility samples

In zero magnetic field, the temperature dependences of the resistivity in high- and low-mobility samples differ drastically, as shown in Fig. 5. In the “metallic” range of densities, ns>ncn_{s}>n_{c}, the resistivity of high-mobility (∼30×103\sim 30\times 10^{3} cm2/Vs) samples varies sharply by a factor of about 7 [30, 31]. In contrast, for low-mobility samples (∼(1−2)×103\sim(1-2)\times 10^{3} cm2/Vs), ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) varies by only ≈15%\approx 15\%, and the variation occurs at much higher temperatures and densities [32]. These well-known features have been explored and explained in Refs. [33, 32, 34, 35, 36].

The upturn at low temperatures in Fig. 5(b) is due to quantum corrections, which for low-mobility samples have an “insulating” sign at all densities (see Fig. 5(b) and Ref. [32]). For high-mobility samples, the upturn is expected to set in upon lowering the temperature below T=h/kB​τT=h/k_{B}\tau and T=h/kB​τvT=h/k_{B}\tau_{v} (here τv\tau_{v} is the intervalley scattering time). This low-temperature regime is outside the range shown in Fig. 5(a).

3.2 Scaling of the resistivity

A notable feature of the resistivity ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependences across various electron densities is that the data can be made to overlap by scaling along the temperature axis. In other words, resistivity can be expressed as a function of T/T0T/T_{0}, where T0T_{0} depends solely on the carrier density, nsn_{s}. This scaling is valid over a wide interval of electron densities around nc≈0.95×1011n_{c}\approx 0.95\times 10^{11} cm-2, specifically for |δ​ns|≲2.5×1010|\delta n_{s}|\lesssim 2.5\times 10^{10} cm-2 (here δ​ns=ns−nc\delta n_{s}=n_{s}-n_{c}), and within the temperature interval of 0.2 to 3 K [31]. The results of the scaling are illustrated in Fig. 6(a), which shows ρ\rho plotted as a function of T/T0T/T_{0}. The data collapse into two distinct curves: the upper curve, represented by open symbols, corresponds to the insulating side of the transition, whereas the lower curve, shown with filled symbols, corresponds to the metallic side. Line thickness primarily reflects the within-dataset scatter, highlighting the high quality of the scaling results. The scaling parameter, T0T_{0}, is shown as a function of nsn_{s} in Fig. 6(b). On both sides of the transition, the scaling parameter obeys a power law dependence T0∝|δ​ns|γT_{0}\propto|\delta n_{s}|^{\gamma} with γ=1.60±0.1\gamma=1.60\pm 0.1 for the insulating side of the transition and γ=1.62±0.1\gamma=1.62\pm 0.1 for the metallic side, and tends to zero as ns→ncn_{s}\rightarrow n_{c}. It is noteworthy that a similar scaling behavior was previously reported in Ref. [37] for the insulator-superconductor transition in thin films of bismuth.

An alternative way to scale the R⁡(T)R(T) curves is to plot them as a function of |δ​ns|/Tb|\delta n_{s}|/T^{b}, as shown in Fig. 7:

ρ⁡(T,ns)=f1​(|δ​ns|/Tb)\rho(T,n_{s})=f_{1}(|\delta n_{s}|/T^{b}) (3)

Here b=1/z​κb=1/z\kappa, zz is the dynamical exponent, and κ\kappa is the correlation length exponent [38]. This method allows one to find the product of the dynamical and the correlation exponents [39]. More on this will be discussed below.

The remarkable reflection symmetry of the two branches in the scaled ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependences shown in Figs. 6 and 7 relative to ncn_{c} indicates an approximately symmetrical empirical description of ρ⁡(T,ns)\rho(T,n_{s}), as suggested by Pudalov [40]:

ρ⁡(T)\displaystyle\rho(T) =\displaystyle= ρ0+ρ1exp(−Δ(ns)/T),\displaystyle\rho_{0}+\rho_{1}\exp(-\Delta(n_{s})/T),
Δ⁡(ns)\displaystyle\Delta(n_{s}) =\displaystyle= λ⁡(ns−nc),\displaystyle\lambda(n_{s}-n_{c}), (4)

where λ\lambda is a phenomenological parameter. This empirical form is discussed in more detail in Section 10.4.

Note that there are both similarities and differences between the metal-insulator transition and the superconductor-insulator transition. For superconductor-insulator transitions, two scenarios are considered: the fermionic scenario, in which the order parameter amplitude vanishes, and the bosonic scenario, in which the amplitude of phase fluctuations reaches a critical value. This diversity is absent in the case of the metal-insulator transition, at least in the current state of knowledge. On the other hand, similarities include, for example, mirror symmetry between the two phases in the critical regime and a tendency toward phase separation that strengthens as the critical point is approached by varying the control parameter (disorder or carrier density).

3.3 Nonlinear effects

The data reported in Refs. [30, 31] were obtained in the linear regime, i.e., in the limit of the zero electric field, E→0E\rightarrow 0. Typical current-voltage (I−VI-V) curves across the metal-insulator transition are shown in Fig. 8. The middle, solid curve is close to linear and separates all I−VI-V curves into two groups exhibiting different types of nonlinear behavior. Note that there is a remarkable symmetry about the middle curve. This symmetry is reminiscent of that observed for the I−VI-V curves in the vicinity of the quantum Hall liquid to insulator phase transition [41]. Curves of resistivity vs. the electric field for different electron densities are shown in Fig. 9. Again, there is clearly a critical electron density that separates two distinct density regions characterized by different types of resistivity behavior as a function of the electric field. At the critical point, the resistivity (the solid curve in Fig. 8, closed circles in Fig. 9) is virtually independent of the electric field and close to 3​h/e23h/e^{2}. The curves below this line are characterized by d​R/d​E>0dR/dE>0, while all curves above are characterized by d​R/d​E<0dR/dE<0. The observed critical behavior of the resistivity as a function of EE is very similar to the critical behavior of the resistivity with temperature (Fig. 4) with the only difference being that the resistivity at the critical point is independent of the electric field while the metallic R⁡(T)R(T) curves in the close vicinity of the critical electron density are non-monotonic.

A general scaling analysis of the Coulomb-interacting quantum critical point [38] suggests that the resistivity should also scale with the electric field:

ρ⁡(E,ns)=f2​(|δ​ns|/Ea)\rho(E,n_{s})=f_{2}(|\delta n_{s}|/E^{a}) (5)

Indeed, plotting resistivity against the scaling variable, |δ​ns|/Ea|\delta n_{s}|/E^{a}, collapses all curves onto two distinct branches [39], as shown in Fig. 10 (here a=1/(z+1)​κa=1/(z+1)\kappa). At the transition, the resistivity is close to 3​h/e23h/e^{2}. The quality of the electric-field scaling is considerably higher than that of the temperature scaling. The best collapse was achieved for a=0.37±0.01a=0.37\pm 0.01.

Knowing both z​κz\kappa and (z+1)​κ(z+1)\kappa, it is possible to determine the exponents zz and κ\kappa separately, as was done for the superconductor-insulator transition in thin disordered films [42]. The values obtained in Ref. [39] are z=0.8±0.1z=0.8\pm 0.1 and κ=1.5±0.1\kappa=1.5\pm 0.1. Although the correlation length exponent has not been theoretically predicted for this system, the dynamical exponent in a strongly interacting 2D system was predicted to be z=1z=1, which is close to what was reported in Ref. [39]. In the majority of interacting 2D systems where it has been determined, the exponent zz has also been found to be close to 1 (Ref. [42] for the case of a superconductor-insulator transition or Ref. [43] for the transition between two neighboring quantum Hall effect plateaus).

3.4 Experiments on other strongly-interacting 2D systems

Initially, these results were met with great skepticism and largely overlooked until 1997, when they were almost simultaneously experimentally confirmed in other strongly interacting 2D electron and hole systems: silicon MOSFETs from a different research group [44], pp-type SiGe structures [45], pp-GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures [46, 47, 48], n−n-type GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures [49], AlAs systems [50], and, more recently, in unprecedentedly clean SiGe quantum wells [51] with the drop of the resistance by a factor of 12 below T≈1.2T\approx 1.2 K and ZnO heterostructures with a fivefold drop of the resistance below ≈100\approx 100 mK [52]. Some of the examples are shown in Figs. 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. The values of rsr_{s} in these studies varied from ≈4\approx 4 [49] to >40>40 [47].

Scaling analysis has been applied to a variety of 2D systems with different degrees of success. Several experiments have produced scaling exponents b=1/z​κb=1/z\kappa ranging from 1.25 to 1.6 for Si MOSFETs [44] and pp-type SiGe systems [45]. In the 2D systems where both temperature and the electric field scaling were attempted, the results for the correlation length exponent ranged between 1.5 and 1.9 [31, 53]. The dynamical exponent varied between 0.8 and 1.2 in Si MOSFETs [31, 53] and was found equal to 1 in pp-SiGe heterostructures [54]. However, attempts to scale the resistivity of pp-type GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures have either resulted in significantly larger exponents [55] or have entirely failed [47]. Generally, it seems that scaling analysis yields larger exponents or breaks down in systems that exhibit relatively weak metallic temperature behavior, as observed in some pp-GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures and low-mobility Si MOSFETs. Conversely, the more pronounced the metallic temperature behavior, the better the scaling fits.

In the most clean and uniform Si MOSFET samples, the resistivity at ns=7.25×1010n_{s}=7.25\times 10^{10} cm-2 has been found to be essentially independent of temperature from approximately 1 K down to about 35 mK [56], the lowest temperature reached in that experiment. It is tempting to identify the corresponding electron density with the critical one for the MIT. Just below this “separatrix” (for “just-metallic” electron densities, ns≳ncn_{s}\gtrsim n_{c}), the resistivity decreases with decreasing temperature down to the lowest accessed temperatures with no indication of an upturn at T→0T\rightarrow 0 (see Fig. 16). Later, a symmetry-based analysis of the resistivity near the critical fixed point [57] suggested a more rigorous definition of the separatrix. This critical ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) curve must have no exponential temperature term, no inflection points, and no maxima. According to such a definition, the critical electron density is nc≈0.88±0.02×1010n_{c}\approx 0.88\pm{0.02}\times 10^{10} cm-2 in Fig. 15 and nc≈7.25×1010n_{c}\approx 7.25\times 10^{10} cm-2 in Fig. 16. We emphasize that the metallic temperature dependence overpowers quantum localization. However, the transport behavior in the limit as TT approaches 0 requires more thorough consideration, which will be presented in Section 4.

In ultra-clean pp-GaAs 2D systems, the resistivity shows no upturns at least down to 25 mK [48]. Fig. 17 shows ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) over the range 25 mK - 10 K for 9 different hole densities. In the limit of low temperatures, the resistance becomes either constant (7 lower curves) or continues to decrease (two upper curves).

4 Suppression of the coherent backscattering near the MIT

It turns out that the weak localization corrections, which exist deep in the metallic phase, weaken as one approaches the transition and practically vanish at the critical density. In Ref. [58], the weak-field negative magnetoresistance was studied in Si MOSFETs (see Fig. 18), and its magnitude was found to decrease by a factor of 50 compared to its “noninteracting” value upon approaching ncn_{c} from the metallic side of the transition. The same conclusion was reached for ultraclean pp-GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures with very low carrier densities (down to 7×1097\times 10^{9} cm-2; rs≈24r_{s}\approx 24), suggesting that the effects of coherent backscattering are suppressed at such low densities and, as a consequence, in the presence of strong interactions [59]. Relatively far from the transition, the corrections to the conductivity due to coherent backscattering are consistent with their non-interacting values, as was reported earlier [60]. However, once the transition is approached (δ​ns/nc≲0.1\delta n_{s}/n_{c}\lesssim 0.1; rs≈20r_{s}\approx 20), the corrections become progressively weaker, and in the immediate vicinity of the critical density, they practically vanish.

An alternative theoretical explanation for the decrease in the weak-localization prefactor as the metal-insulator transition (MIT) is approached was proposed in Ref. [61]. This explanation is based on the failure of the conventional Hikami-Larkin first-order expansion in 1/G1/G as the dimensionless conductance GG decreases. Including second-order corrections has been shown to reduce the weak-localization prefactor.

5 Equivalence of two approaches for determining the critical point in zero magnetic field

To determine the limiting behavior at zero temperature experimentally, one can follow two principal approaches: extrapolating the temperature dependence of the conductivity or resistance to T=0T=0 or analyzing temperature-independent characteristics (e.g., the correlation length). Since zero temperature is inaccessible, comparing different criteria provides an experimental test to assess whether a true MIT exists. As previously mentioned, the separatrix between metal and insulator in high-mobility silicon and pp-GaAs samples remains either slightly tilted or flat down to the lowest accessible temperatures, with no signs of divergence. It is tempting to extrapolate the separatrix to T=0T=0 and identify the corresponding electron density as the critical density for the metal-insulator transition. However, like any extrapolation to T=0T=0, this approach should be justified. Therefore, an independent determination of the critical point is required. This is why in Ref. [62], the critical density obtained by an extrapolation criterion was compared with that obtained by a temperature-independent method.

The first criterion based on the extrapolation to zero temperature is a change in sign of the temperature derivative of the resistivity, d​ρ/d​Td\rho/dT. A positive (negative) sign of the derivative at the lowest achievable temperatures is empirically associated with a metallic (insulating) phase. The second criterion is based on a vanishing activation energy, EaE_{a}, combined with a vanishing nonlinearity (threshold voltage, VcV_{c}) of the current-voltage characteristics when extrapolated from the insulating phase [26]. The activation energy and the threshold voltage are connected via the localization length, which is temperature-independent. While the derivative method deals with the vicinity of the MIT in which the dependence ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) is flat, the I−VI-V method is related to the insulating phase with an exponential ρ⁡(T)\rho(T). These two methods have been applied simultaneously to the 2D MIT in Ref. [62].

The resistivity as a function of temperature is shown in Fig. 19 for several electron densities on both sides of the metal-insulator transition. The resistivity of the middle (dashed) curve shows virtually no temperature dependence over a wide range of temperatures and separates those with positive and negative d​ρ/d​Td\rho/dT nearly symmetrically (at temperatures above 0.2 K) as reported earlier [63, 56]. Assuming that the middle curve remains flat down to T=0T=0, we obtain the MIT critical point at 0.795×10110.795\times 10^{11} cm-2 which corresponds to a resistivity ρ≈3​h/e2\rho\approx 3h/e^{2}, as in other experiments on Si MOSFETs [64, 56]. We designate the so-determined electron density as the critical density, nc​1n_{c1}.

The MIT point has also been determined by studying the behavior of nonlinear I−VI-V characteristics on the insulating side of the transition. Deep in the insulating state (ns<nc​1n_{s}<n_{c1}), a typical low-temperature I−VI-V curve is close to a step-like function: the voltage rises abruptly at low current and then saturates, as shown in Fig. 20. The magnitude of the step is 2​Vc2\,V_{c}. At higher temperatures, the curve becomes less sharp, yet the threshold voltage, VcV_{c}, remains practically unchanged. Closer to the MIT, the I−VI-V curves still show a nonlinear step-like behavior provided that ns<nc​1n_{s}<n_{c1} (see the curve in Fig. 20(b) corresponding to ns=0.743×1011n_{s}=0.743\times 10^{11} cm-2). Exactly at ns=nc​1=0.795×1011n_{s}=n_{c1}=0.795\times 10^{11} cm-2, the I−VI-V curve is strictly linear; at ns>nc​1n_{s}>n_{c1}, it becomes superlinear, which is characteristic of the metallic state [39]. Figure 21 (closed circles) shows that the square root of the threshold voltage is a linear function of electron density. Extrapolation of the Vc1/2​(ns)V_{c}^{1/2}(n_{s}) dependence to zero threshold value yields the critical electron density nc​2n_{c2}. Note that nc​2n_{c2} is equal to nc​1n_{c1} with high accuracy.

Not too deep on the insulating side of the transition, and at not too low temperatures, the resistance has an activated form [26, 65], as shown in the inset to Fig. 20(a). (At lower temperatures, the activated ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) transforms into the Efros-Shklovskii hopping [15]. Note also that in the immediate vicinity of the transition, ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependences are not activated but rather reflection-symmetric about the transition.) Such a form of temperature dependence was interpreted in Ref. [66] as a result of the thermal activation of carriers to the mobility edge, EcE_{c}; in this case, the activation energy is Ea=Ec−EFE_{a}=E_{c}-E_{F}. Since in the insulating regime, the I−VI-V curves are strongly nonlinear, the resistivity was determined from d​V/d​IdV/dI in the linear interval of I−VI-V curves, i.e., at I→0I\rightarrow 0. Figure 21 shows EaE_{a} as a function of the electron density (open circles). In previous detailed studies [26], this dependence was found to be linear near the mobility edge (deeper in the insulating state, the density of states decreases as compared to its value in the vicinity of the transition, which results in an increase in the slope of the Ea​(ns)E_{a}(n_{s}) dependence). The present data can also be approximated by a linear function which yields, within the experimental uncertainty, the same critical electron density nc​2n_{c2} as the square root of the threshold voltage. The reciprocal slope of Ea​(ns)E_{a}(n_{s}), D∗D^{*}, can be interpreted [66] as the thermodynamic density of states near the transition point.

The breakdown occurs when the localized electrons at the Fermi level gain enough energy to reach the mobility edge in an electric field, Vc/dV_{c}/d, over a distance given by the localization length, LL: e​Vc​L/d=Ec−EFeV_{c}L/d=E_{c}-E_{F}, where dd is the distance between the potential probes [26]. The values EaE_{a} and VcV_{c} are related through the localization length, which is temperature-independent and diverges near the transition as L⁡(EF)∝(Ec−EF)−sL(E_{F})\propto(E_{c}-E_{F})^{-s} with exponent ss close to unity [26]. This corresponds to a linear dependence Vc1/2​(ns)V_{c}^{1/2}(n_{s}) [67, 68, 26] near the MIT, as seen in Fig. 21.

We stress that, in a zero magnetic field, both methods — extrapolating ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) to zero temperature and using the behavior of the temperature-independent localization length — yield the same critical electron density. This adds confidence that the curve with zero derivative d​ρ/d​Td\rho/dT will remain “flat” (or at least will retain a finite resistivity value) down to zero temperature. It is important to note that in Ref. [68], the density dependence of the threshold electric field, given by Et∝(δ​ns)3/2E_{t}\propto(\delta n_{s})^{3/2}, was explained within the framework of the pinned Wigner solid based on the quantum tunneling of dislocations. For more details on the nonlinear threshold transport in the pinned Wigner solid, see section 9.

6 The effect of a parallel magnetic field

We now consider the effect of a field B∥B_{\parallel} applied parallel to the 2D plane. A parallel field couples only to electron spins and not to their orbital motion (provided that the fields are not so high that the magnetic length becomes comparable to the thickness of the 2D system). The first observation of a suppression of conductivity in low-density Si MOSFETs by B∥B_{\parallel} was reported in Ref. [69], in which the cut-off criterion (the resistivity either smaller or higher than 100 kΩ\Omega) was used to separate the metallic and insulating states on the (B,nsB,n_{s}) plane. Magnetoresistance in a parallel magnetic field was studied in detail in Refs. [70, 71] in Si MOSFETs (see Figs. 22, 23). With increasing B∥B_{\parallel}, the resistance increases by a factor of a few deep in the metallic state and then saturates at a constant value at a density-dependent field Bs​a​tB_{sat} (see three bottom curves in Fig. 23), but when the application of B∥B_{\parallel} promoted the insulating state, the resistance increased by orders of magnitude before saturating (Figs. 22, 23). Later, in Refs. [72, 73], it was shown that Bs​a​tB_{sat} corresponds to the onset of a complete spin polarization: measurements in magnetic fields applied at small angles relative to the 2D plane indicated a factor of two increase in the frequency of Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) oscillations at B≥Bs​a​tB\geq B_{sat}.

The effect of a parallel magnetic field is qualitatively similar in pp-GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures [74, 75]. An example is shown in Fig. 24. However, ρ⁡(B∥)\rho(B_{\parallel}) does not saturate to a constant value as in Si MOSFETs, but instead continues to increase with increasing field, albeit at a considerably slower rate. As in Si MOSFETs, a distinct knee demarcates behavior in low and high fields. Unlike in Si MOSFETs, magnetoresistance in pp-GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures is anisotropic, depending on the relative orientations of the measuring current, magnetic field, and crystal axes. These effects were studied in detail in Ref. [75]. In this system, there may be a contribution to the magnetoresistance anisotropy depending upon the angle between the current and the magnetic field due to the finite thickness of the 2D layer, as proposed in Ref. [76].

As shown in Fig. 25, a parallel magnetic field suppresses the metallic behavior and eventually turns the zero-field metal into a high-field insulator for densities up to at least 1.4​nc1.4\;n_{c} [77]. The separatrix resistance, which is temperature-independent and close to 3​h/e23h/e^{2} in zero field, acquires a strongly (by orders of magnitude) insulating temperature dependence at T≲1T\lesssim 1 K in a parallel field of only 1 tesla. Thus, the localized behavior, which is absent at ns≥ncn_{s}\geq n_{c} in B=0B=0, is “restored” in a parallel magnetic field [69, 70, 71, 74, 75]. In contrast, the same field has a negligible effect on the resistance at temperatures higher than 1 K where the resistance can be described by the Drude formula.

If the electron densities significantly exceed ncn_{c}, where R<<h/e2R<<h/e^{2} at B=0B=0, the complete spin polarization causes the increase of the resistance by a factor of 4 [78], not leading to localization of electrons as long as R⁡(Bs​a​t)R(B_{sat}) remains below h/e2h/e^{2}. In general, the critical electron density for the Anderson MIT increases with the parallel magnetic field due to the effects of exchange and correlations [79]. This is in agreement with the conclusions of Refs. [80, 81, 82] where it was shown that the increase in the number of spin and valley degrees of freedom promotes the metallicity.

Finally, we would like to mention that the metallic temperature dependence of the resistance, although weaker than that in the B=0B=0 case, still survives in a completely spin-polarized (“spinless”), two-valley electron system in ultra-clean SiGe/Si/SiGe heterostructures [83]. This is in contrast to the above-described results obtained on more disordered two-valley silicon samples, in which a spin-polarizing magnetic field completely quenches metallic temperature behavior. The fact that the spinless electrons behave differently in ultra-clean systems in SiGe/Si/SiGe quantum wells as compared to those in Si MOSFETs can be attributed to different intervalley scattering rates: while the intervalley scattering due to the irregularities of the interface in Si MOSFETs mixes the two valleys to effectively produce a single valley at low temperatures, the level of short-range disorder potential in SiGe/Si/SiGe samples is some two orders of magnitude lower than that in the least disordered Si MOSFETs, hence the intervalley scattering rate is small compared to that in Si MOSFETs, corresponding to the case of two distinct valleys. The critical electron density, nc​(Bs​a​t)n_{c}(B_{sat}), for the MIT in the spinless electron system in SiGe/Si/SiGe quantum wells is higher by a factor of about 1.2 compared to nc​(0)n_{c}(0), which is consistent with theoretical calculations [79]. The observed metallic temperature behavior in spinless SiGe/Si/SiGe systems is comparable to that in strongly interacting, spin-unpolarized single-valley 2D systems in the cleanest pp-type GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures, which indicates the same role of spins and distinct valleys with respect to the existence of the metallic state and the MIT.

7 The effect of quantizing perpendicular magnetic fields

In a strong perpendicular magnetic field, B⊥B_{\bot}, samples at electron densities below and just above ncn_{c} exhibit rather complex magnetoresistance. As reported in Refs. [23, 84, 65], the diagonal resistance first increases strongly with B⊥B_{\bot}, sometimes by orders of magnitude (see Figs. 26 and 27). At higher B⊥B_{\bot}, the magnetoresistance turns negative, and eventually the system exhibits giant resistance oscillations with deep minima at magnetic fields corresponding to Landau level filling factors ν=1\nu=1 and 22 and a maximum in between (often referred to as the “reentrant behavior”). However, the Hall resistance follows the classical dependence Rx​y​(B)R_{xy}(B) (the so-called Hall insulator [85, 86]) despite Rx​xR_{xx} reaching values exceeding h/e2h/e^{2} by orders of magnitude between the integer filling factors 6 and 2 and between 2 and 1 (Fig. 27(a), (b)). At ν=2\nu=2 and ν=1\nu=1, Rx​yR_{xy} takes on quantized integer quantum Hall effect values of h/2​e2h/2e^{2} and h/e2h/e^{2}, respectively [84, 87]. Similar features in ρx​x​(B)\rho_{xx}(B) dependences have been observed in pp-GaAs quantum wells [88], as shown in Fig. 28.

The application of the perpendicular magnetic field affects the critical density of the MIT. Magnetic field dependences of the longitudinal resistivity in SiGe/Si/SiGe heterostructures are shown in the inset to Fig. 29. The resistivity minimum at the Landau level filling factor ν=ns​h​c/e​B=1\nu=n_{s}hc/eB=1 survives down to electron densities near the MIT. This is similar to the re-entrant behavior that was discussed in the previous paragraph, observed earlier in Si MOSFETs and GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures [84, 89, 90, 24, 88]. The resulting phase diagram is shown in Fig. 29. The critical electron density increases with B⊥B_{\bot} at low magnetic fields and then, at the Landau filling factor ν=1\nu=1, decreases to a value below that for B=0B=0. At higher magnetic fields (in the extreme quantum limit), it monotonically grows and exhibits a knee at ν=2/5\nu=2/5. Indeed, in this electron system, the longitudinal resistance minimum at ν=2/5\nu=2/5 is stronger than that at ν=1/3\nu=1/3 (see Ref. [91]), in contrast to the strongly-interacting 2D hole system in a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure [92]. The boundary then continues to grow with a slope corresponding to ν≈0.3\nu\approx 0.3. This is different from the slope of ν≈0.5\nu\approx 0.5 observed in Si MOSFETs in the extreme quantum limit [89] and interpreted as a consequence of the localization of electrons below half-filling of the lowest Landau level. For comparison, the slope of the high-field boundary in pp-type GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures is intermediate (i.e., ν≈0.38\nu\approx 0.38; see Ref. [88]). Based on the results obtained in these strongly interacting carrier systems, the authors of Ref. [51] arrived at the conclusion that the critical density for the MIT in the extreme quantum limit is likely to be determined by the level of disorder.

8 Measurements of the renormalized electron parameters: spin susceptibility and the effective mass

As discussed in the previous section, the behaviors of spin-unpolarized and spin-polarized strongly interacting 2D systems differ drastically. This underscores the essential role of electron spins in two-dimensional metal-insulator transitions and encourages the investigation of magnetic properties.

8.1 Transport measurements

In Ref. [84, 65, 93], Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations were studied in Si MOSFET samples in perpendicular magnetic fields in a wide range of electron densities. The authors reported that near the metal-insulator transition, only “spin” minima in the resistance are observed at Landau filling factors ν=\nu= 2, 6, 10, and 14, whereas the “cyclotron” minima at ν=\nu= 4, 8, and 12 disappear. This behavior was observed in a rather broad range of magnetic fields. It was interpreted as a giant (by a factor of ∼5\sim 5) enhancement of the product, g∗​m∗g^{*}m^{*}, of the gg-factor and the effective mass near the metal-insulator transition. 22 2 Throughout this paper, we prefer to use quasiparticle parameters such as the renormalized effective mass m∗m^{*}, spin susceptibility χ\chi, etc., even though these parameters differ substantially from the band values in a strongly correlated electron system. This is done within a standard approach without discussing the applicability of the Fermi liquid concept when it can successfully describe the observed phenomena.

Indirect measurements of the spin susceptibility of 2D electron systems in Si MOSFETs were made in Ref. [94]. The authors studied low-temperature magnetoresistance ρ⁡(B)\rho(B) in a parallel magnetic field (see Fig. 30) and found, in agreement with earlier measurements [71, 70, 72, 73], that the resistivity increases approximately quadratically with the field until it saturates at a constant value above a certain density-dependent magnetic field, Bs​a​tB_{sat}, corresponding to the onset of a complete spin polarization. In the vicinity of the metal-insulator transition, magnetoresistance strongly depends on temperature, as reported, e.g., in Ref. [95]. However, as one moves away from the transition deep into the metallic state, this temperature dependence weakens and eventually disappears at very low temperatures. The data discussed in Ref. [94] were obtained in this low-temperature limit, where the magnetoresistance becomes temperature-independent.

In Fig. 31, we illustrate how the magnetoresistance curves, shown in Fig. 30, collapse onto a single curve after being normalized by ρ⁡(0)\rho(0) and plotted as a function of B/Bs​a​tB/B_{sat}. The scaling parameter, Bs​a​tB_{sat}, has been normalized to the magnetic field at which the magnetoresistance saturates and, hence, the electrons reach full spin polarization [72, 73]. The observed scaling is remarkably good for B/Bs​a​t≤0.7B/B_{sat}\leq 0.7 in the electron density range 1.08×1011−1×10121.08\times 10^{11}-1\times 10^{12} cm-2, although with increasing nsn_{s} the scaled experimental data occupy progressively shorter intervals on the resulting curve. At both B/Bs​a​t>0.7B/B_{sat}>0.7 and outside the indicated range of electron densities, the scaled data start to noticeably deviate from the universal curve. In particular, the scaling breaks down as one approaches the metal-insulator transition (ns<1.3​ncn_{s}<1.3\,n_{c}), which in this sample occurs at zero magnetic field at nc=8×1010n_{c}=8\times 10^{10} cm-2. We note that the observed scaling dependence is described reasonably well by the theoretical dependence of ρ/ρ⁡(0)\rho/\rho(0) on the degree of spin polarization

ξ=g∗​m∗​μB​B/π​ℏ2​ns=B/Bs​a​t\xi=g^{*}m^{*}\mu_{B}B/\pi\hbar^{2}n_{s}=B/B_{sat} (6)

(where both the gg-factor g∗g^{*} and the effective mass m∗m^{*} may be enhanced due to interactions) as predicted in Ref. [78] based on the spin polarization-dependent screening of a random potential deep within the metallic regime.

In Fig. 32, it is shown that with high precision, Bs​a​tB_{sat} is proportional to the deviation of the electron density from its critical value, i.e., to δ​ns\delta n_{s}, over a wide range of electron densities. In other words, the field at which the magnetoresistance saturates and the complete spin polarization is reached tends to vanish at ncn_{c}. Note that at nsn_{s} above 2.4×10152.4\times 10^{15} m-2, the saturation of the resistance is not reached in the available magnetic field range. Still, the high precision of the collapse of the high-density experimental curves onto the same scaling curve as the low-density data allows one to draw conclusions about the validity of the obtained law Bs​a​t​(ns)∝δ​nsB_{sat}(n_{s})\propto\delta n_{s} over a much wider range of electron densities.

The fact that the saturation (or polarization) field tends to vanish at ncn_{c} would be trivial if the density of the delocalized electrons approached zero at the metal-insulator transition. However, the studied least-disordered samples are remarkable for the smallness of the band tail of localized electrons down to electron densities ns≈1×1011n_{s}\approx 1\times 10^{11} cm-2. This follows from the coincidence of the full spin polarization field obtained from parallel-field magnetotransport and that obtained from the analysis of the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations, because the former is influenced by a possible band tail of localized electrons including singly-occupied states [96] that leads to shifting the Bs​a​t​(ns)B_{sat}(n_{s}) dependence to higher densities, whereas the latter is not [96, 97, 98, 99, 100]. In samples with a relatively high critical density ncn_{c} for the B=0B=0 MIT, the field Bs​a​tB_{sat} decreases, and the band tail of localized electrons increases. In this case, the crucial region of low electron densities falls within the insulating regime where the physics of local moments dominates. Indeed, in those samples, a sublinear magnetic-field dependence of the magnetization characteristic of local moments has been predicted, and the extracted spin susceptibility is expected to have a Curie temperature dependence [96]. This dependence holds even at high electron densities, where metallic behavior might be expected. Note that the band tail of localized electrons contributes to the measured magnetization owing to the presence of empty states below the Fermi level.

Based on the data shown in Fig. 32 and the above form of the spin polarization parameter ξ\xi, the ratio of the product g∗​m∗g^{*}m^{*} to g0​m0g_{0}m_{0} can be calculated (here g0=2g_{0}=2 and m0=0.19​mem_{0}=0.19m_{e} is the band mass in Si). The dependence g∗​m∗/g0​m0​(ns)g^{*}m^{*}/g_{0}m_{0}(n_{s}) is shown in Fig. 33. Upon approaching the critical density ncn_{c}, the spin susceptibility increases by a factor of about five compared to its “noninteracting” value 2​m02m_{0}.

Another approach to determining the spin susceptibility in Si MOSFET samples was proposed in Ref. [104]. The authors measured Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in superimposed, independently controlled parallel and perpendicular magnetic fields across a wide range of electron densities, including the vicinity of the MIT, and determined the spin susceptibility, the effective mass, and the gg-factor of mobile electrons. The results are displayed in Fig. 34. For small rsr_{s}, g∗​m∗/g0​m0g^{*}m^{*}/g_{0}m_{0} values agree with the earlier data by Okamoto et al. [72]. For rs≥6r_{s}\geq 6, the ratio g∗​m∗/g0​m0g^{*}m^{*}/g_{0}m_{0} increases with rsr_{s} faster than it might be expected from extrapolation of the results of Ref. [72] and reaches ∼5\sim 5, consistent with the results of Refs. [93] and [94]. Depending on two different methods for determining m∗m^{*}, the renormalized effective mass grows near the MIT by a factor of ≈2.5\approx 2.5 (open circles in Fig. 34) or ≈2\approx 2 (closed circles) compared to its band value, and the renormalized gg-factor grows by a factor of ≈1.7\approx 1.7 or ≈2.2\approx 2.2, respectively.

An independent way to separate g∗g^{*} and m∗m^{*} was used in Ref. [105]. Using the theory of interaction-driven corrections to conductivity [106], the authors extracted from the transport data the Fermi liquid constants, F0aF_{0}^{a} and F1sF_{1}^{s}, responsible for the renormalization of the gg-factor (g∗/g0=1/(1+F0a)g^{*}/g_{0}=1/(1+F_{0}^{a})) and the effective mass (m∗/m0=1+F1sm^{*}/m_{0}=1+F_{1}^{s}). It turns out that the effective mass is strongly enhanced as the electron density decreases, while the gg-factor remains nearly constant. The results are shown in Fig. 35. At relatively high electron densities, ns≳4×1011n_{s}\gtrsim 4\times 10^{11} cm-2 (lower rsr_{s}), the enhancement of both g∗g^{*} and m∗m^{*} is relatively small, both values slightly increasing with decreasing electron density, in agreement with previous data [107]. Also, the renormalization of the gg-factor is dominant compared to that of the effective mass, which is consistent with theoretical results [108, 109, 110]. In contrast, the renormalization in the low nsn_{s} (critical) region, where rs≫1r_{s}\gg 1, is much more striking. As the electron density is decreased, the renormalization of the effective mass overshoots abruptly while that of the gg-factor remains relatively small, g∗≈g0g^{*}\approx g_{0}, without tending to increase. Hence, the results of Ref. [105] indicate that it is mainly the effective mass that is responsible for the drastically enhanced χ∝g∗​m∗\chi\propto g^{*}m^{*} near the metal-insulator transition. At low electron densities, the effective mass determined from analysis of SdH oscillations in tilted magnetic fields is found to be independent of the degree of spin polarization, indicating that the mass enhancement is not related to the electrons’ spins [111, 112, 113].

8.2 Magnetization and magnetocapacitance measurements

A new method for measuring the thermodynamic spin magnetization of a 2D electron system was used in Refs. [101, 114, 115, 116]. The method involved modulating the magnetic field parallel to the 2D plane at a low frequency, thereby modulating the chemical potential of the 2D electron system and measuring the induced current, the imaginary (out-of-phase) component of which is equal to

i=(2​π​f​C​Bm​o​d/e)​∂μ/∂B,i=(2\pi fCB_{mod}/e)\,\partial\mu/\partial B, (7)

where CC is the capacitance of the gated structure and μ\mu is the chemical potential. Applying the Maxwell relation ∂M/∂ns=−∂μ/∂B\partial M/\partial n_{s}=-\partial\mu/\partial B, one can obtain the magnetization MM from the measured current. The measured ∂M/∂n\partial M/\partial n at 9 T magnetic field and T=100T=100 mK is depicted by dots in Fig. 36(a). The sample is a Si MOSFET with relatively high nc=1.25×1011n_{c}=1.25\times 10^{11} cm-2 for the B=0B=0 MIT [101]. The smooth solid line depicts the same quantity as extracted from Shubnikov-de Haas data in Si MOSFETs [104]. The difference between the two curves is attributed to the diamagnetic shift and to the presence of localized spins. The spin magnetization over the entire density range is obtained by subtracting the diamagnetic contribution (dashed line) from the measured data (dots); the latter is small compared to the spin contribution. The spin magnetization (Fig. 36(b)) at a given field is obtained by numerical integration of the extracted ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s} values over nsn_{s}.

The spin magnetization at various magnetic fields and four temperatures is depicted in Fig. 37. For each magnetic field, the curves with higher magnetization values correspond to lower temperatures. The thick blue line corresponds to full polarization of all carriers at a given density, and the thick red line corresponds to the zero-temperature magnetization of a non-interacting degenerate electron gas at B=6B=6 T. The empty circles denote, for each magnetic field, the critical density for the MIT, nc​(B)n_{c}(B). At high magnetic fields, the full spin alignment persists up to densities considerably higher than those predicted for non-interacting electrons.

The inverse susceptibility, determined from B=0.7B=0.7 T spin magnetization, normalized by the electron density, is depicted as a function of temperature in Fig. 38. The susceptibility measured at densities just below ncn_{c} approaches the free-spin value (Curie law). Note that χ\chi in the metallic phase depends on temperature down to 0.1 K. This dependence indicates the existence of a relevant energy scale considerably smaller than the Zeeman one (dashed vertical line in Fig. 38). The authors suggested that such an energy scale may arise from localized spins that interact very weakly with each other.

The thermodynamic spin susceptibility χT\chi_{T} probed in the low-field regime B<kB​T/g​μBB<k_{B}T/g\mu_{B} increases upon cooling (see Fig. 38), which is clearly inconsistent with the spin susceptibility of the Fermi gas (thick black line) or of a Fermi liquid. The increase persists across the overall range of densities and indicates the involvement of localized states both well above and below the critical density ncn_{c}. The localized states occupy an energy interval at the bottom of the potential well, below the band of extended states (band tail) [1, 96]. When these states are treated as free spins, the susceptibility is expected to be proportional to 1/T1/T. As shown in Ref. [117], interactions between localized spins lead to antiferromagnetic coupling and to a susceptibility that grows slower than 1/T1/T. These expectations contradict the experimental results presented in Fig. 39, where χT\chi_{T} varies as 1/Tα1/T^{\alpha} with α=1−2\alpha=1-2 [101, 118]. Subsequent measurements [116] have shown that the low-field slope of ∂M/∂ns∝∂χT/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s}\propto\partial\chi_{T}/\partial n_{s} changes sign between the regions ns>ncn_{s}>n_{c} and ns<ncn_{s}<n_{c} (dashed line in Fig. 40(d)). In higher fields, the linear field dependence of ∂μ/∂B=−∂M/∂ns\partial\mu/\partial B=-\partial M/\partial n_{s} at ns=2×1011n_{s}=2\times 10^{11} cm-2 saturates at B∗≈0.5B^{*}\approx 0.5 T (see Fig. 40(d)).

It was later confirmed experimentally [118, 119] and supported theoretically [120] that the strong temperature dependence of the thermodynamic susceptibility, χT​(T)\chi_{T}(T), arises from localized spin droplets. To avoid confusion, we note that these are not related to the droplets introduced by Spivak and Kivelson [121].

8.2.1 Measurements in low B∥B_{\|} fields

More detailed low-field magnetization measurements [118] have shown that the magnetically responsive localized states have an average spin J≈2J\approx 2 (see Fig. 41) and may thus be viewed as collective spin-droplets comprising four electrons. The ability to recharge these states down to the lowest temperatures (0.4 K in Refs. [101, 118]) without any signs of temperature-activated behavior already indicates that these states lie very close to the Fermi energy, according to Pudalov [119]. It was established in Ref. [103] that charge carriers are exchanged between collective localized states and mobile states — at least down to 0.1 K and in a temperature-independent manner — via tunneling (for further details, see Figs. 40 and 41, and also Section 10.4). This finding provides strong evidence that collective localized states coexist with mobile states at the Fermi level, as illustrated in the schematic diagram in Fig. 40(c) (for more detail, see Section 10.4). The authors of Ref. [118] concluded that the temperature-dependent susceptibility, χT\chi_{T}, arises from easily polarizable spin droplets, increases faster than 1/T1/T as temperature decreases, and that the number of spin droplets also increases as ∼1/T\sim 1/T.

In turn, the spin susceptibility of itinerant electrons, extracted from Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in low fields (B<kB​T/g∗​μBB<k_{B}T/g^{*}\mu_{B}), exhibits a weak temperature dependence that is consistent with Fermi liquid theory, according to Pudalov et al. [102]. Furthermore, from the SdH measurements [103], χ\chi was found to vary sharply with the in-plane magnetic field, as Fig. 41 illustrates. The variations of δ​χ​(B)/χ⁡(0)\delta\chi(B)/\chi(0) range from approximately 25% at low densities to around 6% at high densities (specifically, 10×101110\times 10^{11} cm-2). The data presented in Ref. [103] align with the χ⁡(B=0)\chi(B=0) values reported in Refs. [36, 103] when considering the limit as B∥B_{\parallel} approaches 0. The minimum of χ⁡(B)\chi(B) occurs at B∥≈1B_{\parallel}\approx 1 T, for electron densities between (1.1−2)×1011(1.1-2)\times 10^{11} cm-2. This field is significantly weaker than the field of approximately 20 T required to achieve complete spin polarization of the two-dimensional system.

In Figure 40(a), it can be observed that at low densities, the derivative ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s} becomes positive. In all cases, this value is significantly higher than what is expected for the Pauli spin susceptibility. As the magnetic field increases — while still remaining below the thermal energy condition (g​μB​B<kB​Tg\mu_{B}B<k_{B}T) — the value of ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s} rises sharply. At low temperatures, it even exceeds the Bohr magneton by more than a factor of two. More on this is discussed in Section 10.4.1.

A potential reason for these variations is the effect of disorder, which is inevitably present in all material systems. Its characteristics (whether long-range or short-range) and magnitude can differ between samples from different manufacturers. Even a robust parameter like the spin susceptibility of itinerant electrons, denoted as χ\chi, is significantly affected by the nature of the disorder, as established through both experimental [122] and theoretical [123] studies. Weak short-range disorder is known to promote the formation of Wigner crystals by creating a gap in their phonon spectrum [124, 125]. In contrast, long-range disorder tends to increase effective electron-electron interactions, thereby facilitating local Stoner instability [126, 127, 128] and localized Wigner crystallization [129] in confined geometries, such as those found in mesoscopic quantum dots. Additionally, the thickness of the 2D layer and the depletion charge, which can vary across different 2D samples, also influence the renormalization of spin susceptibility [123, 130]. The same dependence applies to spin magnetization. Interestingly, the nonlinear χ⁡(B∥)\chi(B_{\|}) dependence (Fig. 41) holds even at high electron densities, where one might typically expect metallic behavior.

8.2.2 Measurements in higher B∥B_{\|} fields

Such effects have not been observed in much less disordered samples, in which the band tail of localized electrons is small, and the magnetization in the partially-polarized regime exhibits a proportional dependence on the magnetic field [114], as discussed below.

A typical experimental trace of i⁡(ns)i(n_{s}) in a parallel magnetic field of 5 T, measured in Ref. [114], is shown in Fig. 42. The inset shows magnetization M⁡(ns)M(n_{s}) in the metallic phase obtained by integrating dM/dns=−dμ/dBdM/dn_{s}=-d\mu/dB with the integration constant M⁡(∞)=B​χ0M(\infty)=B\chi_{0}, where χ0\chi_{0} is the Pauli spin susceptibility of non-interacting electrons. The onset of complete spin polarization — the electron density npn_{p} at which the electrons start to fill the upper spin subband — is given by the condition d​μ/d​B=0d\mu/dB=0 (M⁡(ns)M(n_{s}) reaches a maximum), as indicated by the black arrow in the figure.

In Fig. 43(a), a set of curves for the experimental d​μ/d​Bd\mu/dB versus electron density in different magnetic fields is shown. The onset of full spin polarization shifts to higher electron densities as the magnetic field increases. The gray area represents the insulating phase, which expands somewhat with BB. The range of magnetic fields is restricted from below by the condition that d​μ/d​Bd\mu/dB crosses zero in the metallic regime. In Fig. 43(b), these curves, normalized by magnetic field, collapse in the partially-polarized regime onto a single “master curve”. Integration of the master curve over nsn_{s} yields spin susceptibility χ=M/B\chi=M/B, as shown in the inset to Fig. 43(b). Also shown is the spin susceptibility obtained by integrating the raw curves at B=B= 1.5, 3, and 6 tesla, which, within experimental error, yield the same dependence.

Yet another method for measuring npn_{p} and χ\chi relies on analyzing the magnetocapacitance, CC. Experimental traces C⁡(ns)C(n_{s}) are shown in Fig. 44(a) for different magnetic fields. As the magnetic field is increased, a step-like feature emerges on the C⁡(ns)C(n_{s}) curves and shifts to higher electron densities. This feature corresponds to the thermodynamic density of states abruptly changing when the electrons’ spins become completely polarized. To see the step-like feature more clearly, in Fig. 44(b), the C⁡(ns)C(n_{s}) curves for different magnetic fields are subtracted from the reference B=0B=0 curve.

In Fig. 45, we show the summary of the results for the Pauli spin susceptibility as a function of nsn_{s}, obtained using all three methods described above. There is good agreement between these results and the data obtained from the transport experiments reported in Ref. [94]. This adds credibility to the transport data and confirms that full spin polarization occurs at the field BcB_{c}. However, evidence for the phase transition can only be obtained from thermodynamic measurements. Moreover, the magnetization data extend to lower densities than the transport data, and larger values of χ\chi are reached, exceeding the “non-interacting” value χ0\chi_{0} by almost an order of magnitude. The Pauli spin susceptibility behaves critically close to the critical density ncn_{c} for the B=0B=0 metal-insulator transition:

χ∝ns/(ns−nχ).\chi\propto n_{s}/(n_{s}-n_{\chi}). (8)

The same technique was used to study thermodynamic magnetization in perpendicular and tilted magnetic fields [115]. By measuring ∂μ/∂B\partial\mu/\partial B at non-integer filling factors, the authors directly determined the spectral characteristics without fitting or adjustable parameters. The results confirmed that the gg-factor is weakly enhanced and practically independent of the electron density down to the lowest densities reached (≈1.5×1011\approx 1.5\times 10^{11} cm-2), whereas the cyclotron mass is strongly enhanced at low nsn_{s}.

8.3 Thermopower

Yet another way to estimate the behavior of the effective mass is to measure the thermoelectric power. Thermopower is defined as the ratio of the thermoelectric voltage to the temperature difference S=−ΔV/ΔTS=-\Delta V/\Delta T. Based on Fermi liquid theory, Dolgopolov and Gold [131, 132] obtained the following expression for the diffusion thermopower of strongly interacting 2D electrons in the low-temperature regime:

S=−β​2​π​kB2​m∗​T3​e​ℏ2​ns,S=-\beta\frac{2\pi k_{B}^{2}m^{*}T}{3e\hbar^{2}n_{s}}, (9)

where kBk_{B} is the Boltzmann constant. This expression, which resembles the well-known Mott relation for non-interacting electrons, was shown to hold in the strongly interacting case, provided one includes the parameter β\beta, which depends on both disorder [133, 134, 135] and interaction strength [131, 132]. The dependence of β\beta on the electron density is rather weak, and the main effect of the electron-electron interactions is to suppress the thermopower SS.

According to Eq. (9), (−S/T)(-S/T) is proportional to m∗/nsm^{*}/n_{s} and, therefore, the thermopower measurements should yield the effective mass. The divergent behavior of diffusion thermopower in Si MOSFETs was reported in Ref. [136] for a more disordered sample and in Ref. [137] for the least-disordered sample, where transport-determined ncn_{c} is the lowest across all samples studied. When plotted as the inverse quantity, (−1/S)(-1/S), versus the electron density (see Fig. 46(a)), in the least-disordered sample it extrapolates to zero at ns=nt=7.8±0.1×1010n_{s}=n_{t}=7.8\pm 0.1\times 10^{10} cm-2, which is close to (or the same as) the density for the metal-insulator transition in this sample (nc≈8×1010n_{c}\approx 8\times 10^{10} cm-2), obtained from the resistance measurements.

Figure 46(b) shows the ratio (−T/S)(-T/S) plotted as a function of nsn_{s} in the least-disordered sample. The data collapse onto a single curve, demonstrating that the thermopower SS is linear in temperature. In turn, the ratio (−T/S)(-T/S) is a function of electron density nsn_{s} of form:

(−T/S)∝(ns−nt)x.(-T/S)\propto(n_{s}-n_{t})^{x}. (10)

Fits to this expression indicate that the thermopower diverges with decreasing electron density with a critical exponent x=1.0±0.1x=1.0\pm 0.1. The measured ratio (−T/S)(-T/S), shown in Fig. 46(b), decreases linearly with decreasing electron density, extrapolating to zero at ntn_{t} and indicating an increase of the effective mass by more than an order of magnitude. The results thus imply divergence of the electron mass at ntn_{t}: m∗∝ns/(ns−nt)m^{*}\propto n_{s}/(n_{s}-n_{t}) — the behavior that is typical in the vicinity of an interaction-induced phase transition. Importantly, a re-plot of the thermopower data obtained in the more disordered sample [136], shown in the lower inset of Fig. 46(b), demonstrates that (−T/S)(-T/S) extrapolates to the same density ntn_{t} as in the least-disordered sample [137] despite a higher critical density for the MIT obtained from the resistance data. Thus, while the electron density of the resistive transition, ncn_{c}, varies with the level of disorder, the divergence of the thermopower and the effective mass occurs at a density ntn_{t} that is independent of the disorder and is governed by the strength of the inter-electron interactions. The thermopower experiments on the least-disordered samples [137] include data for electron densities much closer to the critical point than those accessible with the techniques described above. The effective electron mass m∗≈5​mem^{*}\approx 5\;m_{e}, obtained from thermopower measurements in Ref. [137], significantly exceeds values from previous transport experiments.

The thermopower, as well as the conductivity, provides a measure of the mass at the Fermi level, while the Zeeman field Bs​a​tB_{sat} required to fully polarize the spins measures the mass associated with the bandwidth, which is the Fermi energy measured from the band bottom. For ns≥1011n_{s}\geq 10^{11} cm-2, the mass determined by different methods was found to be essentially the same [99, 100, 112]. On the other hand, the behavior is different at the densities reached in the experiment in the very close vicinity of the critical point ntn_{t} (ns<1011n_{s}<10^{11} cm-2) where the bandwidth-related mass was found to increase by only a factor ≈4\approx 4. This follows from the fact that the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in the dilute 2D electron system in silicon reveal one switch from cyclotron to spin minima (the ratio of the spin and cyclotron splittings reaches ≈1\approx 1) as the electron density is decreased [93], the spin minima surviving down to ns≈ncn_{s}\approx n_{c} [84, 102, 138]. In effect, while the bandwidth does not decrease appreciably in the close vicinity of the critical point ntn_{t} and the effective mass obtained from such measurements does not exhibit a true divergence, the thermopower measurements yield the effective mass at the Fermi energy, which does indeed diverge (see also Section 10.4).

The divergence of the effective mass has been predicted by a number of theories: using Gutzwiller’s theory [139]; using an analogy with He3 near the onset of Wigner crystallization [140, 121]; extending the Fermi liquid concept to the strongly-interacting limit [141]; solving an extended Hubbard model using dynamical mean-field theory [142]; from a renormalization group analysis for multi-valley 2D systems [81]; by Monte-Carlo simulations [143, 144]. Some theories predict that the disorder is important for the mass enhancement [81, 143, 144]. In contrast with most theories that assume a parabolic spectrum, the authors of Ref. [141] stress that there is a clear distinction between the mass at the Fermi level and the bandwidth-related mass. In this respect, our conclusions are consistent with the model of Ref. [141] in which a flattening at the Fermi energy in the spectrum leads to a diverging effective mass. This Fermi-liquid-based model implies the existence of an intermediate phase preceding Wigner crystallization.

8.4 Entropy

The effective electron mass in 2D electron systems can also be extracted from the measurements of the entropy per electron, ∂S∗/∂ns\partial S^{*}/\partial n_{s}. According to the Maxwell relation

(∂S∗/∂n)T=−(∂μ/∂T)ns,(\partial S^{*}/\partial n)_{T}=-(\partial\mu/\partial T)_{n_{s}}, (11)

the sought-for entropy can be found from the temperature derivative of the chemical potential, μ\mu. In order to measure ∂μ/∂T\partial\mu/\partial T of the 2D electron layer, a gated structure, where the 2D electrons and the gate act as two plates of a capacitor, was used [145]. When the temperature is modulated at a frequency ω\omega, the chemical potential of the 2D layer varies, causing the capacitor to recharge. The induced current is equal to

i⁡(t)=∂μ∂T​Δ​T​ω​Ce​sin⁡(ω​t).i(t)=\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial T}\,\Delta T\,\frac{\omega\,C}{e}\sin(\omega t). (12)

The extracted effective mass for different temperatures is shown in Fig. 47. In the high-temperature limit T≫EFT\gg E_{F}, the kinetic energy of electrons is set by temperature, and the 2D electron gas turns out to be weakly interacting, with the density-independent effective mass close to the band mass m0m_{0}. For a given temperature, the effective mass exhibits a reentrant behavior: as density decreases, m∗m^{*} first grows, then passes through a maximum, and falls down approaching a value of the order of m0m_{0} in the low-density non-degenerate (EF≲TE_{F}\lesssim T) regime. The lower the temperature, the higher the maximum effective mass, reaching approximately 5​m05\,m_{0}. The enhanced effective mass is in qualitative agreement with the low-temperature Shubnikov-de Haas measurements [104] shown by a solid curve in Fig. 47. The similarity of the data from different measurement methods justifies the validity of the analysis employed. It is still unclear why the m∗​(ns)m^{*}(n_{s}) peak exceeds the SdH data by a factor of up to 2.5. This “overshooting” could indicate the beginning of band flattening (see section 8.5), but this interpretation has not yet been explored.

8.5 Indication of band flattening

The experimental data obtained in strongly correlated 2D electron systems can be divided into two groups: (i) data describing the electron system as a whole, like thermodynamic density of states, magnetization of the electron system, or the magnetic field required to fully polarize electron spins, and (ii) data related only to the electrons at the Fermi level, like the amplitude of the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations. This yields the effective mass mF∗m^{*}_{F} and Landé gg-factor gF∗g^{*}_{F} at the Fermi level.

Usually, the data in the first group are interpreted using the language of quasiparticles, in which the energy-averaged effective mass, m∗m^{*}, and Landé gg-factor, g∗g^{*}, are used. To determine the values, the formulas for non-interacting electrons are used. Although this approach is not ideologically correct, the results for m∗m^{*} and g∗g^{*} are often the same as, or close to, those for mF∗m^{*}_{F} and gF∗g^{*}_{F}. For example, a simultaneous increase of the energy-averaged effective mass and that at the Fermi level in Si MOSFETs was reported in publications described in previous sections [99, 100, 146].

In contrast, the situation is different in ultra-clean SiGe/Si/SiGe samples [147]. The behavior of the product gF∗​m∗g^{*}_{F}m^{*} of the Landé factor at the Fermi level (where gF∗≈2g^{*}_{F}\approx 2) and the average effective mass differs from that of the product gF∗​mF∗g^{*}_{F}m^{*}_{F} of the Landé factor and the effective mass at the Fermi level. This difference is illustrated in Fig. 48. At high electron densities, the dependences of gF∗​m∗​(ns)g^{*}_{F}m^{*}(n_{s}) and gF∗​mF∗​(ns)g^{*}_{F}m^{*}_{F}(n_{s}) are nearly identical. However, they diverge significantly at low densities: while gF∗​m∗​(ns)g^{*}_{F}m^{*}(n_{s}) saturates, gF∗​mF∗​(ns)g^{*}_{F}m^{*}_{F}(n_{s}) increases monotonically as the electron density decreases across the entire range of nsn_{s}, with a tendency to diverge at low densities.

These experimental results can be interpreted within the concept of the condensation of fermions [148, 149, 150]. The fermion condensation occurs at the Fermi level in a range of momenta, unlike the condensation of bosons. As the strength of electron-electron interactions increases, the single-particle spectrum flattens in a region Δ​p\Delta p near the Fermi momentum pFp_{F} (top inset to Fig. 48). At relatively high electron densities (ns>0.7×1015n_{s}>0.7\times 10^{15} m-2), this effect is not important because the single-particle spectrum does not change noticeably in the interval Δ​p\Delta p, and the behaviors of the energy-averaged effective mass and that at the Fermi level are similar. However, decreasing the electron density in the range ns<0.7×1015n_{s}<0.7\times 10^{15} m-2 stimulates the flattening of the spectrum so that the effective mass at the Fermi level, mF=pF/VFm_{F}=p_{F}/V_{F}, continues to increase (here VFV_{F} is the Fermi velocity). In contrast, the energy-averaged effective mass does not increase and is not particularly sensitive to this flattening.

9 The insulating side of the MIT: transport evidence for sliding Wigner solid

As described in previous sections, experimental investigations into the transport and thermodynamic properties of 2D electrons in semiconductors have indicated that these systems may approach a phase transition to an unknown collective state at low electron densities. This new state could be a quantum Wigner crystal or a precursor [151, 152, 153, 94, 105, 154, 121, 114, 137, 147, 155]. Weak disorder is known to facilitate the formation of the pinned Wigner solid [124, 156]; quantum Monte Carlo calculations [124] that account for realistic disorder have predicted a critical rsr_{s} significantly lower than rs=37r_{s}=37 predicted for the ideal clean 2D system [153]. The phase transition point in the least-disordered 2D electron systems in semiconductors is near the critical electron density for the metal-insulator transition. Although the insulating regime of the metal-insulator transition has been extensively studied [157, 158, 159, 160, 161, 65, 67, 162, 88, 163, 164, 165, 52, 166, 167], there has been no definitive conclusion regarding the origin of the low-density state. Single-threshold current-voltage (I−VI-V) curves have been observed, which can be interpreted either as a sign of the depinning of an electron solid [159, 158, 65, 67] or as a breakdown of the insulating phase, consistent with traditional scenarios like strong electric field Efros-Shklovskii variable range hopping [168] or percolation (see, e.g., Refs. [161, 89, 26, 100] and the references therein). Attempts to observe broadband voltage noise at the threshold of these I−VI-V curves and to probe the low-density state in perpendicular magnetic fields have not yielded sufficient information to clearly differentiate between the depinning of the electron solid and traditional mechanisms [161, 26, 100]. It is important to note that much confusion has arisen because many authors have chosen to interpret their data in the context of the Wigner crystal, overlooking conventional interpretations.

A significant breakthrough in understanding the origin of the low-density state in strongly interacting 2D electron systems has been reported in Ref. [169]. Two-threshold V−IV-I characteristics have been observed, marked by a dramatic increase in noise between the two threshold voltages at the breakdown of the insulating low-electron-density state. This noise manifests itself as strong current fluctuations; it rises significantly above the first threshold voltage Vt​h​1V_{th1} and essentially disappears above the second threshold voltage Vt​h​2V_{th2}.

Figure 49 illustrates a series of low-temperature voltage-current curves measured at different electron densities within the insulating regime in a Si MOSFET sample [169]. The critical density for the MIT in this electron system is approximately nc≈8×1010​cm−2n_{c}\approx 8\times 10^{10}\,\text{cm}^{-2} which corresponds to the interaction parameter rs∼20r_{s}\sim 20. For electron densities below approximately 6×1010​cm−26\times 10^{10}\,\text{cm}^{-2}, two threshold voltages are observed. As the applied voltage increases, the current remains near zero until it reaches a first threshold voltage, Vt​h​1V_{{th1}}. Once Vt​h​1V_{{th1}} is surpassed, the current rises sharply until a second threshold voltage, Vt​h​2V_{{th2}}, is reached. Beyond Vt​h​2V_{{th2}}, the slope of the voltage-current curve decreases significantly, and the behavior becomes linear, although it is not ohmic (see also the top inset of Fig. 49). As the electron density is increased, the value of Vt​h​1V_{{th1}} decreases, while the second threshold becomes less pronounced and eventually disappears.

Figure 50(a) displays the V−IV-I characteristics for the electron density of ns=5.36×1010n_{s}=5.36\times 10^{10} cm-2 at various temperatures. As the temperature TT increases, the second threshold voltage, Vt​h​2V_{{th2}}, becomes less distinct, and the threshold behavior of the V−IV-I curves blurs.

The measured broadband noise is presented as a function of voltage in Fig. 50(b) for various temperatures, with an electron density of ns=5.36×1010​cm−2n_{s}=5.36\times 10^{10}\,\text{cm}^{-2}. A significant increase in noise is observed between the thresholds Vt​h​1V_{{th1}} and Vt​h​2V_{{th2}} at the lowest temperature. This substantial noise decreases rapidly as the temperature increases, which is consistent with the two-threshold behavior seen in the V−IV-I curves shown in Fig. 50(a).
