There is a striking similarity between the double-threshold V−IV-I dependences in the insulating state of Si MOSFETs and those (with the voltage and current axes interchanged) known for the depinning of the vortex lattice in type-II superconductors (see, for example, Refs. [170, 171, 172]). The physics of the vortex lattice in type-II superconductors, in which the existence of two thresholds is well known, can be adapted for the case of an electron solid. The transient region between the dynamic (VdV_{d}) and static (VsV_{s}) thresholds corresponds to the collective pinning of the solid. In this region, the pinning occurs at the centers with different energies, and the current is thermally activated:

I∝exp⁡[−U⁡(V)kB​T],I\propto\exp\left[-\frac{U(V)}{k_{B}T}\right], (13)

where U⁡(V)U(V) is the activation energy. The static threshold VsV_{s} signals the onset of the regime of solid motion with friction. This corresponds to the condition

e​E​L=Uc,eEL=U_{c}, (14)

where EE is the electric field and LL is the characteristic distance between the pinning centers with maximal activation energy UcU_{c}. From the balance of the electric, pinning, and friction forces in the regime of solid motion with friction, one expects a linear V−IV-I characteristic that is offset by the threshold VdV_{d} corresponding to the pinning force

I=σ0​(V−Vd),I=\sigma_{0}(V-V_{d}), (15)

where σ0\sigma_{0} is a coefficient. Assuming that the activation energy for the Wigner solid is equal to

U⁡(V)=Uc−e​E​L=Uc​(1−V/Vs),U(V)=U_{c}-eEL=U_{c}(1-V/V_{s}), (16)

one obtains the expression for the current

I={σ0​(V−Vd)​ if ​V>Vsσ0​(V−Vd)​exp⁡[−Uc​(1−V/Vs)kB​T]​ if ​V≤Vs.I=\left\{\begin{array}[]{c}\sigma_{0}(V-V_{d}){\text{ if }}V>V_{s}\\ \sigma_{0}(V-V_{d})\exp\left[-\frac{U_{c}(1-V/V_{s})}{k_{B}T}\right]{\text{ if }}V\leq V_{s}.\end{array}\right. (17)

The fits to the data using Eq. (17) are shown by dashed lines in Figs. 49 and 50(a). As the figures show, the experimental two-threshold V−IV-I characteristics are described well by Eq. (17). The value of UcU_{c} decreases approximately linearly with electron density and tends to zero at ns≈6×1010n_{s}\approx 6\times 10^{10} cm-2 (the bottom inset of Fig. 49). This is in contrast to the vanishing activation energy of electron-hole pairs at ncn_{c} obtained by measurements of the resistance in the limit of zero voltages/currents [62]. Presumably, the vanishing UcU_{c} is related to the minimum number of the strong pinning centers for which the collective pinning is still possible. The fact that the coefficient σ0\sigma_{0} is approximately constant (σ0≈1.6×10−7\sigma_{0}\approx 1.6\times 10^{-7} Ohm-1) indicates that weak pinning centers control the solid motion with friction [171]. Thus, the physics of the vortex lattice, adapted to the case of an electron solid, is relevant to the insulating state of a 2D electron system in silicon.

Similar effects are observed in much less disordered ultra-high-mobility SiGe/Si/SiGe heterostructures, which belong to a different class of 2D systems as inferred from both the level and character of the disorder potential. In Fig. 51(a), typical voltage-current characteristics (upper panel) and the generated noise (lower panel), measured at a temperature of approximately 30 mK, are presented. The measurements were conducted across different electron densities within the insulating regime [173] (see also Fig. 51(b, c) for a more detailed view). These densities are below, but not too close to, the critical density for the MIT nc≈8.8×109​cm−2n_{c}\approx 8.8\times 10^{9}\,\text{cm}^{-2}. At these specific values of nsn_{s}, the interaction parameter rsr_{s} exceeds 20. Between the two threshold voltages, a peak in broadband current noise is observed, as shown in the lower panel of Fig. 51(a). Figure 52 shows how the voltage-current characteristics and noise levels change with temperature. As the temperature rises, the voltage-current characteristics become less steep between the two threshold voltages, and the curves shift to lower voltages until the behavior associated with these two thresholds disappears. Similarly, the noise peak diminishes and eventually disappears as temperature increases. The inset of the upper panel in Fig. 52(a) features an Arrhenius plot of I⁡(T)I(T), which illustrates the activation temperature dependence down to approximately 60 mK.

As in silicon MOSFETs, the observed results can be explained by a phenomenological theory of collective depinning of elastic structures, which naturally produces a peak in broadband current noise between the dynamic and static thresholds, transitioning to the sliding of the solid over a pinning barrier once the static threshold is exceeded. These findings provide evidence for the formation of a quantum electron solid within this electron system and demonstrate the generality of the effect across different classes of electron systems.

10 Modern theoretical approaches to the B=0B=0 MIT

10.1 Metallic temperature dependence of the resistivity

In the mid-80s, the quasi-linear “metallic” temperature dependence of conductivity observed in the ballistic interaction regime (kB​T​τ/ℏ>1k_{B}T\tau/\hbar>1)) was attributed [174, 33, 175] to the weakening of screening of the scattering potential with increasing temperature. More recently, a theory was developed that accounted for all interaction contributions to the conductivity, including exchange contributions [106, 176]. This theory offers a unified approach to both ballistic and diffusive (kB​T​τ/ℏ<1k_{B}T\tau/\hbar<1) interaction regimes by considering quantum interference between electron waves scattered on Friedel oscillations of the electron density. The theories mentioned above provide a quantitative description of the linear-in-TT corrections to the conductivity in the ballistic regime [177]. The theory [106, 176] was extended to the case of a long-range scattering potential [178]. The theories [106, 176, 178] naturally incorporate the Altshuler-Aronov results for the interaction corrections to the conductivity in the diffusive regime [7].

10.2 Two-parameter scaling theory

The low-temperature physics of the disordered electron liquid, combined with the large rsr_{s} values near the MIT, is determined by the properties of interacting, diffusing electrons [9, 11, 10]. A modern scaling theory for the 2D MIT in a disordered two-dimensional electron gas was presented in Ref. [81]. A quantum critical point has been identified that separates the metallic phase, stabilized by electron-electron interactions, from the insulating phase, where disorder prevails over interactions. According to Ref. [81], the existence of a quantum critical point leads to a divergence in the density of states at the transition, causing the thermodynamic properties to exhibit critical behavior as the transition is approached.

The experimental test of this theory was done in Refs. [179, 57]. The authors have performed simultaneous measurements of the resistivity, ρ\rho, and in-plane magnetoconductance, σ⁡(B)\sigma(B). Since the origin of the magnetoconductance lies in the interaction corrections to the conductance involving different spin projections (Hartree-like), the corresponding interaction strength can be determined from the slope of the magnetic field dependence of conductivity σ⁡(B)\sigma(B). When a magnetic field BB is applied parallel to the 2D plane in the diffusive regime, kB​T<ℏ/τ<EFk_{B}T<\hbar/\tau<E_{F} [180, 8], the magnetoconductance Δ​σ​(B,T)≡σ⁡(B,T)−σ⁡(0,T)\Delta\sigma(B,T)\equiv\sigma(B,T)-\sigma(0,T) is proportional to b2b^{2} in the weak field limit b≡g​μB​B/kB​T≪1b\equiv g\mu_{B}B/k_{B}T\ll 1. On the other hand, at higher temperatures ℏ/τ<kB​T<EF\hbar/\tau<k_{B}T<E_{F}, referred to as the ballistic regime, Δ​σ​(B,T)\Delta\sigma(B,T) is expected to be proportional to T​b2Tb^{2} [176]. Due to the significant difference in magnetoconductivities between these two regions, measuring Δ​σ​(B,T)\Delta\sigma(B,T) provides a method to identify the diffusive regime, although some accompanying difficulties were reported in Ref. [181].

The explicit form of the slope of Δ​σ​(b2)\Delta\sigma(b^{2}) for the single valley case was derived in Refs. [180, 182] and generalized to include the valley degrees of freedom in Ref. [179]. In the case when there are nvn_{v} degenerate valleys (nv=2n_{v}=2 for silicon), the authors obtained for Δ​σ​(b2)\Delta\sigma(b^{2}), in the limit b≪1b\ll 1, the expression

Δ​σ​(b2)=−0.091​e2π​h​nv2​γ2​(γ2+1)​b2.\Delta\sigma(b^{2})=-0.091\frac{e^{2}}{\pi h}n_{v}^{2}\gamma_{2}\left(\gamma_{2}+1\right)b^{2}. (18)

Here, γ2\gamma_{2} is the effective electron-electron interaction amplitude in the spin-density channel.

Eq. (18), as was shown in Ref. [182], incorporates renormalization group (RG) corrections to first order in ρ\rho and is therefore strictly valid only deep in the metallic region. However, for general ρ\rho, the magnetoconductance in the diffusive regime will still retain the b2b^{2}-form, Δ​σ=−(e2/π​h)​Ce​e​(γ2,ρ)​nv2​b2\Delta\sigma=-(e^{2}/\pi h)\,C_{ee}(\gamma_{2},\rho)\,n_{v}^{2}\,b^{2}. The coefficient Ce​eC_{ee} reflects the strength of spin-related interactions at any value of the resistance, as long as g​μB​B<kB​T<h/τg\mu_{B}B<k_{B}T<h/\tau [179].

The temperature dependences of the parameter Ce​eC_{ee}, extracted by fitting the σ⁡(b2)\sigma(b^{2}) traces shown in Fig. 53, are displayed in Fig. 54(b) for various densities across the MIT. In Fig. 54(a), ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependences at zero magnetic field for the same densities are plotted. Fig. 54 reveals that not only ρ\rho but also the interaction strength exhibits a fan-like spread as the MIT is crossed. While the interaction increases in the metallic phase as the temperature decreases, it is suppressed in the insulating phase. The magnitudes of these changes depend on the distance from the MIT, with both ρ\rho and γ2\gamma_{2} becoming practically temperature-independent for densities near the MIT.

To see this in a different way, the authors of Ref. [179] combined Figs. 54(a) and (b) and constructed a two-parameter “flow” diagram in the disorder–interaction (Ce​e−ρC_{ee}-\rho) space. This flow diagram is presented in Fig. 55. One can see that it clearly indicates the existence of a quantum critical point from which three separatrices, one attractive and two repulsive, can be drawn.

On the metallic side of the flow diagram, a separatrix that forms the envelope of a family of non-monotonic curves is clearly visible in Fig. 55 and flows toward the region with ρ≪1\rho\ll 1. The theoretical details of the evolution of ρ\rho and γ2\gamma_{2} in this region with ρ≪1\rho\ll 1 were discussed in detail in Ref. [80] in terms of the renormalization group (RG) theory. We recall the salient features of the theory here. The theory predicts that:
(i) The amplitude γ2\gamma_{2} increases monotonically as the temperature is reduced.
(ii) The resistance, on the other hand, has a characteristic non-monotonic form changing from insulating behavior (d​ρ/d​T<0d\rho/dT<0) at high temperatures to metallic behavior (d​ρ/d​T>0d\rho/dT>0) at low temperatures, with the maximum value ρm​a​x\rho_{max} occurring at a crossover temperature T=Tm​a​xT=T_{max}.
(iii) The value of the amplitude γ2\gamma_{2} at T=Tm​a​xT=T_{max} is universal in the limit ρm​a​x≪1\rho_{max}\ll 1, depending only on nvn_{v}; for nv=1n_{v}=1, it is 2.082.08, while for nv=2n_{v}=2, it has the much lower value 0.450.45.
(iv) Although the values of ρm​a​x\rho_{max} and Tm​a​xT_{max} are not universal and depend on the system, the behaviors of ρ⁡(T)/ρm​a​x\rho(T)/\rho_{max} and γ2​(T)\gamma_{2}(T) are universal when plotted as functions of ρm​a​x\rho_{max}ln(T/Tm​a​x)(T/T_{max}).

The results of the comparison between experiment and theory are presented in Figs. 56(a) and (b), for the three largest densities in the diffusive regime with ρm​a​x≲0.4​(π​h/e2)\rho_{max}\lesssim 0.4~(\pi h/e^{2}). At these densities, the resistance is small enough, and one can safely extract the interaction amplitudes γ2\gamma_{2} from Δ​σ​(b2)\Delta\sigma(b^{2}) using Eq. (18), i.e., Ce​e=0.091​γ2​(1+γ2)C_{ee}=0.091\gamma_{2}(1+\gamma_{2}). (As the density increases, the maximum in ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) becomes less pronounced, and the non-monotonicity eventually disappears at ns≳1×1011n_{s}\gtrsim 1\times 10^{11} cm-2, as the ballistic region is approached.) The solid lines are the universal theoretical curves for ρ⁡(T)/ρm​a​x\rho(T)/\rho_{max} and γ2​(T)\gamma_{2}(T) plotted as a function of ρm​a​x​ln⁡(T/Tm​a​x)\rho_{max}\ln(T/T_{max}). One sees from Fig. 56 that at T=Tm​a​xT=T_{max}, the value of the interaction amplitude γ2≈0.45\gamma_{2}\approx 0.45, which is in remarkable agreement with theory for nv=2n_{v}=2. The agreement between theory and experiment is especially striking given that the theory has no adjustable parameters. Systematic deviations from the universal curve occur at lower densities as higher-order corrections in ρ\rho become important.

Parameter γ2\gamma_{2} may also be determined from the renormalized g∗g^{*}-factor in the diffusive regime, using, e.g., SdH oscillations:

γ2​(γ2+1)≈g∗2​(1−g∗2).\gamma_{2}(\gamma_{2}+1)\approx\frac{g^{*}}{2}(1-\frac{g^{*}}{2}). (19)

The temperature dependence of the g-factor, and consequently, γ2\gamma_{2}, was determined from weak-field SdH oscillations in the study by Pudalov et al. [102] within a temperature range of 0.1 to 1 K. This analysis was conducted while decreasing the electron density from approximately 7​nc7\,n_{c} to ncn_{c}. The dependence of γ2\gamma_{2} on temperature was found to be weak, with no significant increase at lower temperatures as predicted by the renormalization group (RG) theory. The authors of the study concluded that a key prediction of RG theory — a substantial increase in γ2\gamma_{2} with cooling — was not supported by the SdH measurements.

It has been predicted [81] that the effective mass should dramatically increase at disorder-dependent density for the metal-insulator transition while the g-factor remains nearly intact. However, the prediction of disorder-dependent effective mass is not confirmed by the experimental data [183].

Another method for testing the two-parameter scaling theory is illustrated in the right panel of Fig. 55. In this context, the data should be described by a universal scaling function ℛ⁡(X,Y)\mathcal{R}(X,Y), which represents a two-dimensional surface plotted in the (X,Y,ρ)(X,Y,\rho) space [57]. Here, XX and YY correspond to the normalized deviations in the density (ns−nc)(n_{s}-n_{c}) and the normalized temperature, respectively [57]. The scaling function was reconstructed from experimental data over a wide range of XX and YY values. The data from five different samples were found to collapse onto a single surface in the (X,Y,ρ)(X,Y,\rho) space. This relationship can be expressed as ρ⁡(T,n)ρc0=exp⁡[f1​(X)]​f2​(Y)\frac{\rho(T,n)}{\rho_{c}^{0}}=\exp[f_{1}(X)]f_{2}(Y). The data are very close to the model surface; maximal deviation of the data from the model surface in the ρ\rho direction does not exceed 0.05​ρc00.05\rho_{c}^{0}. Clearly, the surface is curved in both directions, whereas the separatrix ρc​(T)\rho_{c}(T) is represented by the straight line on the model surface.

10.3 Dynamical mean-field theory

The two-parameter scaling theory, which has been very successful in describing experimental results in the diffusive regime (roughly kB​T​τ/ℏ<1k_{B}T\tau/\hbar<1), is applicable only to a narrow range of electron densities near the critical density for the metal-insulator transition. In contrast, the strong changes in the resistivity with temperature are experimentally observed in a wide range of electron densities: up to five times the critical density, including the ballistic regime (roughly, kB​T​τ/ℏ>1k_{B}T\tau/\hbar>1), where the scaling theory is no longer applicable (we stress that the ballistic regime introduced in Ref. [106] is not related to the well-known ballistic transport, or Knudsen regime, where the mean free path is larger than the sample dimensions).

According to Ref. [106], a similar physical mechanism, namely, the elastic but temperature-dependent scattering of electrons by the self-consistent potential created by all other electrons, works in principle in both diffusive and ballistic regimes. However, small corrections calculated in the ballistic regime [106] cannot convincingly account for the order-of-magnitude changes in the resistivity observed in the experiment.

An alternative interpretation of the temperature dependence of resistivity is the so-called Wigner-Mott scenario, which emphasizes the role of strong electron-electron interactions. The simplest theoretical approach to non-perturbatively tackle the interactions as the main driving force for the metal-insulator transition is based on dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) methods of Refs. [184, 185, 186] using the Hubbard model at half filling. On the metallic side near the metal-insulator transition, the resistivity was predicted to initially increase as the temperature is reduced, reach a maximum at temperature Tm​a​x∼TFT_{max}\sim T_{F}, and then decrease as T→0T\rightarrow 0. It was also shown that the resistivity change ρ⁡(T)−ρ⁡(0)\rho(T)-\rho(0), normalized by its maximum value, is a universal function of T/Tm​a​xT/T_{{max}}.

Temperature dependences of the resistivity for two samples in the metallic regime are shown in Fig. 57 in the range of electron densities where the ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) curves are non-monotonic: at temperatures below a density-dependent temperature Tm​a​xT_{{max}}, they exhibit metallic temperature behavior (d​ρ/d​T>0\mathrm{d}\rho/\mathrm{d}T>0), while above Tm​a​xT_{{max}}, their behavior is insulating (d​ρ/d​T<0\mathrm{d}\rho/\mathrm{d}T<0) [187]. Note that the changes in the resistivity with temperature at T<Tm​a​xT<T_{{max}} are strong and may exceed an order of magnitude (more than a factor of 12 for the lowest curve in Fig. 57(b)). The data recalculated into the conductivity as a function of temperature are displayed in the inset of Fig. 57(b). Also shown are linear fits to the data. The observed linear temperature dependence is consistent with the ballistic regime not too close to ncn_{c}. As inferred from the temperature dependence of the conductivity, the transient region between ballistic and diffusive regimes corresponds to electron densities around ≈1.1×1010\approx 1.1\times 10^{10} cm-2.

The results of the scaling of these data for two samples in the spirit of dynamical mean-field theory [184, 185, 186] are shown in Fig. 58. The data scale perfectly over a wide range of electron densities and are well described by theory in the weak-disorder limit; it should be emphasized that at some electron densities, the changes in resistivity with temperature exceed an order of magnitude. Deviations from the theoretical curve arise in the high-temperature limit in the transient region and become pronounced for T>Tm​a​xT>T_{{max}} at electron densities within ∼10\sim 10% of the critical value, which in these samples is close to nc≈0.88×1010n_{c}\approx 0.88\times 10^{10} cm-2. The fact that in the low-temperature limit the same data display linear-in-TT corrections to the conductivity (see the inset in Fig. 57(b)), which are in agreement with both the theory of interaction corrections [106] and the generalized screening theory [177], reveals the consistency of these theories and the DMFT.

For proper perspective and comparison, the authors of Ref. [187] have also performed a scaling analysis in the spirit of the renormalization-group scaling theory [80, 81], according to which the normalized resistivity ρ/ρm​a​x\rho/\rho_{{max}} should be a universal function of the product ρm​a​x​ln⁡(T/Tm​a​x)\rho_{{max}}\ln(T/T_{{max}}) as described in the previous subsection. The results are plotted in Fig. 59. In both samples, only the data obtained at ns=1.18×1010n_{s}=1.18\times 10^{10} cm-2 for sample A (Fig. 59(a)) and at ns=1.17×1010n_{s}=1.17\times 10^{10} cm-2 for sample B (Fig. 59(b)) coincide nearly perfectly with the theoretical curve, although some deviations occur at the lowest temperature. Pronounced deviations from the theory are evident at both higher and lower nsn_{s}. At lower electron densities, the scaled experimental curves are wider than the theoretical curve, and at higher densities, they are narrower. A similar shrinkage of the scaled curves with increasing nsn_{s} was reported earlier in Refs. [80, 179, 185]. One should take into account, however, that theory [80, 81] has been developed for 2D electron systems that, on the one hand, are in the diffusive regime and, on the other hand, their resistivities are low compared to π​h/e2\pi h/e^{2}: at higher values of ρ\rho, higher-order corrections become important and cause deviations from the universal scaling curve. As a result, the parameter space becomes very narrow.

A natural question arises about the connection between DMFT and scaling theory. Both theories predict non-monotonic temperature dependences of the resistivity. Within the renormalization-group scaling theory [80, 81], the maximum in the ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependence occurs at a temperature well below TFT_{F}, at which the temperature-dependent interactions become strong enough to stabilize the metallic state and overcome the effect of the quantum localization. Within the DMFT, in contrast, the maximum corresponds to the quasiparticle coherence temperature T∗∼TFT^{*}\sim T_{F}: below this temperature, the elastic electron-electron scattering corresponds to coherent transport, while at higher temperatures the inelastic electron-electron scattering becomes strong and gives rise to a fully incoherent transport. Even though the theoretical estimates of the positions of the maxima may be crude, the origins of the maxima are clearly different within these two theories in view of the role of the disorder. It should be stressed, on the other hand, that the functional forms of ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependences, including the maximum at Tm​a​x∼TFT_{{max}}\sim T_{F}, expected from both the screening theory in its general form and DMFT, are similar. In particular, the linear temperature dependence of the conductivity at T≪TFT\ll T_{F} following from the generalized screening theory [177] and from the theory of the corrections to the conductivity due to the scattering on Friedel oscillations in the ballistic regime [106] is consistent with the prediction of the DMFT. The similarity of the theoretical predictions adds confidence to both theories and suggests that the underlying microscopic mechanism may be the same, i.e., electron-impurity or impurity-mediated electron-electron scattering in the strongly interacting case, as mentioned above.

Yet another approach to treat the strongly-interacting 2D electron systems, focused on the Pomeranchuk effect expected within a phase coexistence region between the Wigner crystal and a Fermi liquid, was proposed in Refs. [140, 121, 188]. The predicted ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependence is also non-monotonic: the resistivity increases with decreasing temperature at T≳TFT\gtrsim T_{F} and decreases at lower temperatures. However, no quantitative treatment of this problem, capable of quantitative comparison with experiment, currently exists.

In Ref. [189], a Gaussian approximation to the mean-field theory of the second-order phase transition was suggested to describe the 2D MIT. The authors have defined the effective distance to the quantum critical point as the cube of the difference between the critical and actual electron densities. Using this assumption, they analytically found the critical exponent for the divergence of the correlation length, which agrees with the experimental data [31, 190] on both sides of the transition. The phase diagram in the nsn_{s}–TT plane was described as typical of a system exhibiting a quantum phase transition.

10.4 Phase separation in strongly correlated 2D systems

In two-dimensional systems, instability can occur in charge- or spin-exchange channels, leading to the formation of either “ice floes” in the Wigner phase or “spin droplets” in the Stoner phase. Theoretically, Spivak highlighted the importance of phase separation by drawing an analogy with liquid helium-3 [140]. His phenomenological model aligns qualitatively with several experimental observations, including a maximum in resistivity versus temperature, negative compressibility, and the coexistence of spatially separated localized and extended phases in equilibrium.

Various scenarios for a two-phase state have been explored, wherein such phases can emerge in restricted geometries due to local Wigner instability [140, 121], local Stoner instability [191, 126, 192], or changes in the topology of the Fermi surface [148, 141, 193]. It has been suggested in previous studies [140, 188] and further developed in references [194, 195, 196, 197] that the first-order transition from a Fermi liquid to a Wigner crystal is replaced by a series of intermediate “microemulsion” phases. In these phases, the two distinct states coexist within spatially structured domains.

Phase separation signatures in Si MOSFETs were observed through thermodynamic spin-magnetization measurements [118], transport measurements [181, 119], spin susceptibility via oscillatory magnetotransport [138], and quantum oscillations at the electron solid/liquid boundary [84, 65].

In 1997, Pudalov suggested [40] that the additive resistivity functional form (Eq. 4) holds over a wide density range. The function ρ1​(ns,B)\rho_{1}(n_{s},B) decays slowly with respect to nsn_{s}, while ρ0​(ns,T)\rho_{0}(n_{s},T) incorporates both Drude resistivity and quantum corrections, arising from single-particle interference and interactions. Although this empirical form of resistivity was proposed in Ref. [40] based on different principles, it aligns well with the ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) dependence observed in several material systems [40, 46, 50, 198, 199, 200]. This empirical additive form of ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) meets the general criteria for transport behavior near a critical point [201, 57]. On the insulating side of the metal-insulator transition, the resistivity exhibits an exponential temperature dependence. Therefore, this formulation inherently maintains the mirror symmetry of the ρ⁡(ns,T)\rho(n_{s},T) scaling in the vicinity of the MIT. Additionally, this form suggests two-channel scattering, consistent with the two-phase state of low-density two-dimensional electronic systems and in accordance with Matthiessen’s rule.

The experimental data for both ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) and σ⁡(T)\sigma(T), as shown in Fig. 60, exhibit variations so significant that first-order corrections in TT are insufficient to describe them. The simplest functional form represented by Eq. (4) effectively captures the inflection point in ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) and shows the linear relationship between density and the inflection temperature [40]. In this model, the inflection temperature is defined as Ti​n​f​l=Δ/2T_{infl}=\Delta/2. To account for the effects of the magnetic field, all even-order terms in BB and the lowest-order terms in B/TB/T have been included, as follows:

Δ⁡(T,B,n)/T=Δ0​(n)/T−β⁡(n)​B2/T−ξ⁡(n)​B2/T2,\Delta(T,B,n)/T=\Delta_{0}(n)/T-\beta(n)B^{2}/T-\xi(n)B^{2}/T^{2}, (20)

with Δ0=α⁡[n−nc​(0)]\Delta_{0}=\alpha[n-n_{c}(0)].

Equations (4) and (20) link the magnetoconductance with the zero-field ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) temperature dependence. Combining equations (4) and (20), the following ρ⁡(T,B)\rho(T,B) dependence is obtained:

ρ(B,T)=[σD−δσ⋅exp(−T/TB)]−1\displaystyle\rho(B,T)=\left[\sigma_{D}-\delta\sigma\cdot\exp\left(-T/T_{B}\right)\right]^{-1}
+ρ1​exp⁡(−α​n−nc​(0)T−β​B2T−ξ​B2T2)\displaystyle+\rho_{1}\exp\left(-\alpha\frac{n-n_{c}(0)}{T}-\beta\frac{B^{2}}{T}-\xi\frac{B^{2}}{T^{2}}\right) (21)

The term in the square brackets includes the Drude conductivity and interaction quantum corrections [106, 176], which are smoothly cut off above T=TB≈Δ/2T=T_{B}\approx\Delta/2. δ​σ​(T)\delta\sigma(T) was calculated in Ref. [181] using experimentally determined Fermi-liquid coupling constants F0σ​(ns)F_{0}^{\sigma}(n_{s}) [104, 36], and σD\sigma_{D} found by a conventional procedure [104, 36].

From Eq. (21), the prefactor aσ=−12​∂2σ∂B2a_{\sigma}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\sigma}{\partial B^{2}} is calculated straightforwardly and is compared with experimental data in Fig. 60(b, d, f, h). In the fitting of ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) shown in Figs. 60 (a, c, e, g), there is essentially only one adjustable parameter, ρ1​(ns)\rho_{1}(n_{s}), for each density. Notably, nc​(0)n_{c}(0) is determined using conventional scaling analysis at B=0B=0 [57].

Both the electrical resistivity, ρ⁡(T)\rho(T), and aσ=−12​∂2σ∂B2a_{\sigma}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\sigma}{\partial B^{2}}, are well captured by the model, which reproduces the key features of the data. It accurately captures the steep rise in ρ⁡(T)\rho(T), including the inflection point, as well as the kink in the dependence of aσ​(T)a_{\sigma}(T). This kink marks a transition from a low-temperature regime characterized by magnetoconductance, where interactions yield a linear temperature dependence of σ⁡(T)\sigma(T), allowing us to neglect the exponential term. In contrast, the high-temperature regime is characterized by a steep exponential rise in ρ⁡(T)\rho(T), which has a semiclassical origin.

It should be emphasized that neither regime is related to the diffusive regime of interactions. This conclusion casts doubt on early attempts to use two-parameter scaling to describe the magnetoresistance σ⁡(B)\sigma(B) and the temperature dependence ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) within the renormalization group approach.

Thus, within the framework of a phenomenological two-phase model with two scattering channels, it is possible to explain all the observed features in transport and magnetotransport in a parallel field. It is important that their characteristic temperatures are close to the crossover temperature Td​M/d​ns​(ns)T_{dM/dn_{s}}(n_{s}), where the spin magnetization per electron changes sign [118]. Physically, this means that at temperatures below Td​M/d​ns​(ns)T_{dM/dn_{s}}(n_{s}), collective droplets with a large spin (minority phase) “melt” with increasing density. In other words, the electrons added to the Fermi liquid improve screening, thereby promoting the disappearance of spin droplets. At temperatures above Td​M/d​ns​(ns)T_{dM/dn_{s}}(n_{s}), on the contrary, the number of spin droplets increases with increasing density; in this case, the electrons added to the 2D system prefer to combine and form new spin droplets. In Ref. [181], it was concluded that T∗T^{*} may be related to the averaged energy spectrum of the collective localized states.

10.4.1 Phase separation effect in spin susceptibility

Using a vector magnetic field technique with two independent superconducting coils, Pudalov et al. [202, 103] precisely measured and analyzed Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations in various in-plane fields. Earlier [104, 112, 102], the oscillatory component δ​ρx​x\delta\rho_{xx} was shown to be well fitted with conventional Lifshits-Kosevich formula [203, 204, 112, 102]; this enables accurate extraction of the spin susceptibility χ\chi and density of mobile carriers nS​d​Hn_{SdH} from the beating of oscillations. In particular, χ\chi values have been determined with an accuracy of ∼(1−2)%\sim(1-2)\% as a function of the in-plane field.

Figures 41 and 61 show a sharp nonmonotonic dependence of χ\chi on the in-plane field. The characteristic δ​χ​(B)/χ⁡(0)\delta\chi(B)/\chi(0) variations are in the range from ∼25%\sim 25\% at low densities to ∼6%\sim 6\% at high densities 10×101110\times 10^{11}cm-2. The data reported in [103] coincide in the B∥→0B_{\parallel}\rightarrow 0 limit with the χ⁡(B=0)\chi(B=0) values reported in Refs. [104, 36]. The characteristic field of the χ⁡(B)\chi(B)-minimum, B∥∼1B_{\parallel}\sim 1  T for ns=(1.1−2)×1011n_{s}=(1.1-2)\times 10^{11}cm-2, is much weaker than the field of complete spin polarization of the 2D system (B∼20B\sim 20 T). Evidently, in a homogeneous single-phase Fermi liquid the only characteristic field is the field of complete spin polarization.

Pudalov et al. [103] proposed a straightforward thermodynamic model (schematically illustrated in Figs. 40(b,c)) featuring two phases coexisting in equilibrium to explain the observed data. This model has effectively accounted for the results both qualitatively and quantitatively, with certain parameters derived from experimental data. Specifically, the dependence of nF​L​(B)n_{FL}(B) calculated using this model for a representative density of 1.4×10111.4\times 10^{11} cm-2 is shown in Fig. 61(d). The results closely align with the direct experimental data presented in Fig. 61(b), supporting the validity of the two-phase thermodynamic approach. Recently, in the context of Maxwell’s construction for addressing the electrostatics of the two-phase state [205], an upper bound for charge redistribution was estimated to be δ​ns/ns∼0.1%\delta n_{s}/n_{s}\sim 0.1\%, which is reasonably consistent with the experimental findings illustrated in Fig. 61(b). It was also noted in Ref. [206] that the amount of redistributed charge is influenced by the nature of the random potential.

10.4.2 Evidence of the phase separation in thermodynamic spin magnetization

In reference [118], measurements were conducted in weak magnetic fields that were less than the temperature; specifically, g​μB​B≤kB​Tg\mu_{B}B\leq k_{B}T. As shown in Fig. 40(a), at low densities, the derivative of magnetization with respect to the carrier density, ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s}, becomes positive and is significantly larger than what is expected for the Pauli spin susceptibility. As the magnetic field increases (while still remaining below the temperature, g​μB​B<kB​Tg\mu_{B}B<k_{B}T), ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s} exhibits a sharp increase, exceeding the value of the Bohr magneton by more than a factor of two at low temperatures (see Fig. 40(a)). The fact that ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s} surpasses the Bohr magneton indicates a ferromagnetic ordering of the electron spins.

The magnetization curves ∂M/∂ns\partial M/\partial n_{s} (Fig. 40(a)) saturate at a field strength b=μB​B/(kB​T)∼0.25b=\mu_{B}B/(k_{B}T)\sim 0.25, suggesting that the particles responding to the field modulation have spins of 1/(2​b)≈21/(2b)\approx 2, rather than the expected value of 1/2. According to Pudalov [118, 119], this finding offers compelling evidence for the presence of ferromagnetic domains within the two-dimensional paramagnetic Fermi liquid, which are known as “spin droplets”. These spin droplets consist of approximately 4 or more electrons and have a total spin of approximately 2. This interpretation of the experimental data has received theoretical support [120]. Spin droplets have been conceptualized as a type of “quantum dot” embedded within a two-dimensional system, coexisting with it in thermodynamic equilibrium (see Fig. 40(b,c)).

10.4.3 Phase separation effects in reentrant integer QHE-insulator transitions: Quantum oscillations of the electron solid/liquid boundary

The reentrant transition between the electron liquid and electron solid states, which is marked by resistivity changes spanning several orders of magnitude (see Figs. 27, 28), was discovered in 1990 [84]. This effect can also be naturally explained within the framework of the two-phase model. As the perpendicular magnetic field increases, the chemical potential μL\mu_{L} in the liquid phase exhibits quantum oscillations [207, 208, 209] as a function of the magnetic field. To determine the chemical potential in the dilute liquid phase, in Ref. [210] the data on the energy spectrum in silicon at high carrier density and high magnetic field [208, 209] were extrapolated to the low-density range. This extrapolation is based on established relationships of spin, cyclotron, and valley splittings as functions of the magnetic field, along with considerations of level broadening [207]. Figure 62(a) depicts the resulting model of the chemical potential in the liquid phase, μL\mu_{L}, as a function of the magnetic field.

At the same time, the chemical potential in the solid (localized) phase remains constant or changes slowly in response to variations in the magnetic field. To ensure that the chemical potential (μ\mu) is equal in both the solid and liquid phases, the equilibrium average density — especially the critical electron density (rcr_{c}) — will necessarily show quantum oscillations when the magnetic field is varied.

Pudalov [210] modeled the relationship between the equilibrium boundary, or critical density, and the perpendicular magnetic field, B⟂B_{\perp}, by relating the chemical potential to the ground state energy per particle, denoted as Eg=E/nsE^{g}=E/n_{s}. By substituting nsn_{s} with rs=(aB)−1(πns)−1/2r_{s}=(a_{B})^{-1}(\pi n_{s})^{-1/2}, one obtains the expression

(d​μLd​B)​δ​B=12​[∂(ESg−ELg)∂rs]​δ​rs.\left(\frac{d\mu_{L}}{dB}\right)\delta B=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\partial(E^{g}_{S}-E^{g}_{L})}{\partial r_{s}}\right]\delta r_{s}.

In this context, ESgE^{g}_{S} and ELgE^{g}_{L} represent the ground state energies in the solid and liquid phases, respectively, while μS\mu_{S} and μL\mu_{L} denote their corresponding chemical potentials. Eventually,

δ​rs=2​δ​μL​[∂(ESg−ELg)/∂rs]−1.\delta r_{s}=2\delta\mu_{L}[\partial(E^{g}_{S}-E^{g}_{L})/\partial r_{s}]^{-1}. (22)

The last equation allows one to calculate small variations in the critical rsr_{s} value from the known dependence of μL​(B)\mu_{L}(B). The latter (Fig. 62(a)) has been extrapolated from the μL​(B)\mu_{L}(B) oscillations measured in [208, 209] at higher densities, and scaled according to the numerical calculations [124] of the ground state energy: ∂(ESg−ELg)/∂rs≈−0.174​m​e​V\partial(E^{g}_{S}-E^{g}_{L})/\partial r_{s}\approx-0.174{\textrm{m}eV}, at the critical value rsr_{s}=10, for a Si MOSFET sample.

The results of the modeling are plotted in Fig. 62(b) by the short dashed curve. The dots with an interpolating continuous line show direct experimental data taken from [65] and recalculated in the units of rsr_{s}. The saw-tooth shape of the modeling boundary between the liquid and solid phases (Fig. 62(b)) explains the observed reentrant QHE-to-insulator transitions. Indeed, when the average carrier density in a 2D system is fixed (by the constant gate voltage) near ncn_{c} and the magnetic field varies, the system crosses the critical boundary and enters the liquid and solid phase space. As a result, resistance varies dramatically at low temperatures, from exponentially low minima in the QHE regime to exponentially high values in the insulator [65].

In this framework, the minima of Rx​xR_{xx} observed during the reentrant insulating transitions originate from the regular quantum Hall effect. As noted by Pudalov [210], these minima indicate changes in the chemical potential rather than the energy gap (see Fig. 62). As a result, these minima are shifted from their positions at integer filling factors towards higher magnetic fields. This observation is consistent with experimental findings [65].

Since calculations [210] give only the variation in rcr_{c}, the vertical position of the model boundary is poorly defined; in Fig. 62 it was chosen following the Monte-Carlo result of Refs. [124, 212]; rc=10r_{c}=10 at B=0B=0. In the calculation of the dashed curve in Fig. 62, no fitting parameters were used; nevertheless, the agreement with direct measurements of rcr_{c} is quite good, both in the magnitude and phase of the quantum oscillations of the rsr_{s}. This is one more argument in favor of the approach based on the two-phase state. The above empirical approach was supported by recent variational Monte-Carlo calculations of the ground state energy of Wigner crystal [212]. Their results confirm that quantum Hall states penetrate the Wigner crystal region of the ν−B\nu-B phase diagram at integer ν\nu values.

Conclusions

The discovery of the metal-insulator transition in a two-dimensional electron system in high-mobility Si MOSFETs gave a powerful impetus to experimental and theoretical research. The subsequent 30 years have seen great progress in the theory of strongly correlated 2D systems, accompanied by experimental observations of numerous novel effects. It is the interactions between carriers that stabilize the metallic state and lead to a significant increase in the spin susceptibility at low densities, with a tendency to diverge, due to the increase in the effective mass on the metallic side near the MIT. We also review indications of band flattening in ultra-clean 2D systems in SiGe/Si/SiGe heterostructures on the metallic side and the formation of a Wigner solid on the insulating side of the MIT. In the last section, modern concepts and the tendency toward phase separation are discussed. The key question is whether metallic conduction and delocalized states persist as the temperature approaches absolute zero and falls below all relevant relaxation rates, including spin relaxation. We conclude that the promising area of strongly correlated 2D electron systems remains open to future research.
